domains.NBT: Number and Operations in Base Ten

standards.clusterText: Know number names and the count sequence.
standards.text: Count to 100 by ones and by tens.

wi.text: Count to 100 by ones and by tens.
wi.levelDescriptors:
CC Advanced
I can count to 100 by ones, tens, and fives.
I can count backwards from 100 by ones and tens.
I can use my knowledge of counting to solve simple addition and subtraction problems.
I can count objects in the real world and estimate their quantity.
I can apply my counting skills to real-life situations, such as counting the number of steps to climb a staircase or the number of cookies on a plate.

CC At Target
I can count to 100 by ones.
I can skip count by 10s to 100.
I can start counting at any number and count to 100.

CC Approaching
I can count to 50 by ones.
I can skip count by 5s to 50.
I can count forward from a random starting point to 100.

CC Emerging
I can count to 10 by ones.
I can skip count by 2s to 10.

standards.clusterText: Know number names and the count sequence.
standards.text: Count forward beginning from a given number within the known sequence (instead of having to begin at 1).

wi.text: Count forward beginning from a given number within the known sequence (instead of having to begin at 1).
wi.levelDescriptors:
CC Advanced:
I can count forward from a given number beyond the known sequence (e.g., starting at 15 and counting to 25).
I can apply my counting skills to real-life situations, such as counting the number of steps I take to get to school or the number of cars that pass by my house in a minute.
I can explain the strategies I use to count forward from a given number.

CC At Target:
I can consistently count forward from any given number within the known sequence (1-10, 1-20, etc.).
I can use objects to help me count forward from a given number.
I can explain how many objects I counted and how I got my answer.

CC Approaching:
I can count forward from a given number within the known sequence, but I sometimes make mistakes or skip numbers.
I can count forward from a given number within the known sequence, but I need help remembering the starting number. 

CC Emerging:
I can count forward from 1 to 10, but I need to start at 1 each time.
I can count forward from a given number if it is within the first five numbers (1-5).

standards.clusterText: Know number names and the count sequence.
standards.text: Write numbers from 0 to 20. Represent a number of objects with a written numeral 0-20 (with 0 representing a count of no objects).

wi.text: Write numbers from 0 to 20. Represent a number of objects with a written numeral 0-20 (with 0 representing a count of no objects).
wi.levelDescriptors:
CC Advanced:
I can not only write numbers from 0 to 20, but I can also write them in different ways, such as using tally marks or Roman numerals.
I can represent large numbers of objects (beyond 20) with written numerals.
I can use my understanding of numbers to solve simple addition and subtraction problems in real-life situations.
For example, I can figure out how many cookies are left after I eat some, or how many more toys I need to have the same amount as my friend.

CC At Target:
I can confidently write all numbers from 0 to 20.
I can represent any number of objects (0-20) with a written numeral.

CC Approaching:
I can write most numbers from 0 to 20 correctly.
I can represent a number of objects (1-10) with a written numeral, but I may need help with larger numbers.

CC Emerging:
I can write some numbers from 0 to 20, but I often forget or confuse them.
I can sometimes represent a small number of objects (1-5) with a written numeral, but I struggle with larger numbers.

standards.clusterText: Count to tell the number of objects.
standards.text: Understand the relationship between numbers and quantities; connect counting to cardinality.

wi.text: Understand the relationship between numbers and quantities; connect counting to cardinality. When counting objects, say the number names in the standard order, pairing each object with one and only one number name and each number name with one and only one object (one to one correspondence). Understand that the last number name said tells the number of objects counted (cardinality). The number of objects is the same regardless of their arrangement or the order in which they were counted (number conservation). c. Understand that each successive number name refers to a quantity that is one larger and the previous number is one smaller (hierarchical inclusion).
wi.levelDescriptors:
CC Advanced:
I can count a large group of objects quickly and accurately.
I can use my understanding of numbers to solve simple addition and subtraction problems.
I can use my understanding of numbers to compare the quantities of different groups of objects.
I can explain to someone else how to count objects and why it is important to count one-to-one.

CC At Target:
I can count objects in order, one-to-one, without skipping or repeating numbers.
I understand that the last number I say tells me how many objects there are, and I can remember the number.
I know that the number of objects is the same regardless of how they are arranged or the order in which I count them.
I understand that each number name is one more than the previous number and one less than the next number.

CC Approaching:
I can count objects in order, but sometimes I skip a number or say a number twice.
I understand that the last number I say tells me how many objects there are, but I don't always remember the number.
I can see that there are the same number of objects even if they are arranged differently.

CC Emerging:
I can sometimes count objects, but I don't always say the number names in order.
I sometimes forget to count all the objects or count some objects twice.
I don't always understand that the last number I say tells me how many objects there are.

standards.clusterText: Count to tell the number of objects.
standards.text: When counting objects, say the number names in the standard order, pairing each object with one and only one number name and each number name with one and only one object.

standards.clusterText: Count to tell the number of objects.
standards.text: Understand that the last number name said tells the number of objects counted. The number of objects is the same regardless of their arrangement or the order in which they were counted.

standards.clusterText: Count to tell the number of objects.
standards.text: Understand that each successive number name refers to a quantity that is one larger.

standards.clusterText: Count to tell the number of objects.
standards.text: Count to answer “how many?” questions about as many as 20 things arranged in a line, a rectangular array, or a circle, or as many as 10 things in a scattered configuration; given a number from 1–20, count out that many objects.

wi.text: Count to answer "how many?" questions about as many as 20 things arranged in a line, a rectangular array, or a circle, or as many as 10 things in a scattered configuration; given a number from 1-20, count out that many objects.
wi.levelDescriptors:
CC Advanced:
I can count large groups of objects efficiently by using strategies like skip counting or grouping.
I can apply my counting skills to solve real-world problems, such as figuring out how many cookies to bake for a party or how many people are in line at the store.
I can explain my counting strategies and reasoning to others.

CC At Target:
I can count up to 20 objects arranged in a line, rectangular array, or circle.
I can count out any number of objects from 1-20 when given the number.
I can answer "how many?" questions for various arrangements of up to 20 objects.

CC Approaching:
I can count up to 15 objects arranged in a line or rectangular array.
I can count out 5-10 objects when given a number.
I can answer "how many?" questions for simple arrangements of up to 10 objects.

CC Emerging:
I can count up to 10 objects arranged in a line.
I can identify the number of objects in a small group without counting individually.

standards.clusterText: Compare numbers.
standards.text: Identify whether the number of objects in one group is greater than, less than, or equal to the number of objects in another group, e.g., by using matching and counting strategies.

wi.text: Identify whether the number of objects (up to 10) in one group is greater than, less than, or equal to the number of objects in another group, e.g., by using matching and counting strategies.
wi.levelDescriptors:
CC Advanced:
I can compare the number of objects in two groups (up to 10) and solve word problems related to comparing quantities.
I can use my understanding of comparing numbers to estimate the number of objects in a group without counting them all.
I can create my own word problems that involve comparing the number of objects in two groups.

CC At Target:
I can identify whether a group of objects (up to 10) has more, less, or the same number of objects as another group by using matching and counting strategies.
I can explain my reasoning by saying things like "There are 5 apples in this group and 3 apples in that group, so there are more apples in the first group."

CC Approaching:
I can match objects in two groups one-to-one and say which group has more or less based on whether I have any objects left over.
I can count the objects in two groups and say which group has more or less based on the numbers.

CC Emerging:
I can identify that there are more objects in a group when it has more objects than I can count on my fingers.
I can tell which group has fewer objects by looking at the groups and saying which one has "less."

standards.clusterText: Compare numbers.
standards.text: Compare two numbers between 1 and 10 presented as written numerals.

wi.text: Compare two numbers between 1 and 10 presented as written numerals using student generated ways to record the comparison.
wi.levelDescriptors:
CC Advanced:
I can compare two numbers between 1 and 10 and explain the difference between them.
I can apply my understanding of number comparison to solve real-world problems.
I can create my own methods for comparing numbers, such as using place value or mental math strategies.
I can explain my methods to others and justify my reasoning.

CC At Target:
I can accurately compare any two numbers between 1 and 10, regardless of their order.
I can explain my reasoning using clear and precise language.
I can record the comparison using symbols (>, <, =) and student-generated methods (number lines, drawings, manipulatives).

CC Approaching:
I can correctly identify the larger number when comparing two single-digit numbers.
I can use manipulatives or drawings to represent the two numbers and compare them.
I can use informal language and symbols (>, <) to record the comparison.

CC Emerging:
I can identify the two numbers being compared.
I can attempt to compare the two numbers using informal language ("bigger," "smaller").

standards.clusterText: Understand addition as putting together and adding to, and understand subtraction as taking apart and taking from.
standards.text: Represent addition and subtraction with objects, fingers, mental images, drawings, sounds (e.g., claps), acting out situations, verbal explanations, expressions, or equations.

wi.text: Represent addition and subtraction with objects, fingers, mental images, drawings, sounds (e.g., claps), acting out situations, verbal explanations, or numbers. Drawings need not show details but should show the mathematics in the problem.
wi.levelDescriptors:
CC Advanced:
I can use manipulatives to solve addition and subtraction problems beyond 10.
I can write number sentences to represent addition and subtraction problems.
I can apply my understanding of addition and subtraction to real-world situations, such as combining groups of objects or figuring out how many objects are left after sharing.
I can explain my reasoning and strategies for solving addition and subtraction problems.

CC At Target:
I can represent addition and subtraction using objects, fingers, drawings, and numbers within 10.
I can explain my thinking when solving addition and subtraction problems.
I can create drawings that accurately represent the addition or subtraction problem.

CC Approaching:
I can use objects to demonstrate adding and subtracting within 5.
I can draw simple pictures to represent adding and subtracting within 5.
I can explain, in my own words, what happens when we add or subtract objects.

CC Emerging:
I can clap my hands to represent adding two objects together.
I can hold up my fingers to represent taking away one object from a group.

standards.clusterText: Understand addition as putting together and adding to, and understand subtraction as taking apart and taking from.
standards.text: Solve addition and subtraction word problems, and add and subtract within 10, e.g., by using objects or drawings to represent the problem.

wi.text: Solve addition and subtraction word problems, and add and subtract within 10, e.g., by using objects or drawings to represent the problem. See Appendix, Table 1 for specific problem situations and category information.
wi.levelDescriptors:
CC Advanced:
I can solve multi-step addition and subtraction word problems involving numbers up to 10.
I can create my own addition and subtraction word problems.
I can use my knowledge of addition and subtraction to solve real-world problems.
I can explain my thinking clearly and concisely.

CC At Target:
I can solve addition and subtraction word problems involving numbers up to 10.
I can use objects, drawings, and number sentences to represent addition and subtraction problems.
I can explain my thinking when solving addition and subtraction problems.
I can use different strategies to solve addition and subtraction problems.

CC Approaching:
I can solve simple addition and subtraction word problems involving numbers up to 5.
I can use objects or drawings to represent addition and subtraction problems.
I can explain my thinking when solving addition and subtraction problems.

CC Emerging:
I can count objects to find the total number.
I can take away objects from a group and count how many are left.
I can use pictures to represent simple addition and subtraction problems.

standards.clusterText: Understand addition as putting together and adding to, and understand subtraction as taking apart and taking from.
standards.text: Decompose numbers less than or equal to 10 into pairs in more than one way, e.g., by using objects or drawings, and record each decomposition by a drawing or equation (e.g., 5 = 2 + 3 and 5 = 4 + 1).

wi.text: Compose and decompose quantities within 10. Decompose numbers less than or equal to 10 into pairs in more than one way, e.g., by using objects or drawings, and record each decomposition with drawings or numbers. Quickly name the quantity of objects briefly shown in structured arrangements anchored to 5 (e.g., fingers, ten frames, math rack/rekenrek) with totals up to 10 without counting by recognizing the arrangement or seeing the quantity in subgroups that are combined (conceptual subitizing).
wi.levelDescriptors:
CC Advanced:
I can decompose any number less than or equal to 10 into pairs in multiple ways using objects, drawings, or mental math and explain my reasoning.
I can instantly recognize the quantity of objects briefly shown in various arrangements, even those not anchored to 5, with totals beyond 10.
I can apply my understanding of composing and decomposing quantities to solve real-world problems, such as figuring out how many pieces of fruit I need to buy to make a fruit salad for a certain number of people.

CC At Target:
I can decompose any number less than or equal to 10 into pairs in more than one way using objects or drawings and record each decomposition with drawings or numbers.
I can quickly name the quantity of objects briefly shown in structured arrangements anchored to 5 (e.g., fingers, ten frames, math rack/rekenrek) with totals up to 10 without counting by recognizing the arrangement or seeing the quantity in subgroups that are combined.

CC Approaching:
I can decompose most numbers less than or equal to 10 into pairs using objects or drawings.
I can often recognize the quantity of objects briefly shown in structured arrangements up to 10 without counting.
I can sometimes decompose numbers less than or equal to 10 into subgroups that are combined.

CC Emerging:
I can decompose some numbers less than or equal to 5 into pairs using objects or drawings.
I can sometimes recognize the quantity of objects briefly shown in structured arrangements up to 5 without counting.

standards.clusterText: Understand addition as putting together and adding to, and understand subtraction as taking apart and taking from.
standards.text: For any number from 1 to 9, find the number that makes 10 when added to the given number, e.g., by using objects or drawings, and record the answer with a drawing or equation.

wi.text: For any number from 1 to 9, find the number that makes 10 when added to the given number, e.g., by using objects or drawings, and record the answer with a drawing or numbers.
wi.levelDescriptors:
CC Advanced:
I can use objects or drawings to find the missing number that makes 10 when added to a given number from 1 to 9.
I can explain my thinking using words or pictures.
I can apply this skill to real-life situations.
For example, I can use my fingers to figure out how many more cookies I need to eat to have 10 total.

CC At Target:
I can use objects or drawings to find the missing number that makes 10 when added to a given number from 1 to 9.
I can record the answer with a drawing or numbers.
For example, if I see 3 objects, I can draw 7 more objects to show that 3 + 7 = 10.

CC Approaching:
I can identify all numbers from 1 to 9.
I can count objects up to 10.
I can use objects to show that 5 + 5 = 10.

CC Emerging:
I can identify some numbers from 1 to 9.
I can count objects up to 5.

standards.clusterText: Understand addition as putting together and adding to, and understand subtraction as taking apart and taking from.
standards.text: Fluently add and subtract within 5.

wi.text: Flexibly and efficiently add and subtract within 5 using mental images and composing/decomposing numbers up to 5.
wi.levelDescriptors:
CC Advanced:
I can add and subtract within 5 fluently and automatically.
I can apply my understanding of addition and subtraction to solve real-world problems. For example, I can figure out how many cookies are left in a jar after I eat 2 of them.
I can explain my thinking when solving addition and subtraction problems.

CC At Target:
I can add and subtract within 5 using mental images.
I can compose and decompose numbers up to 5. For example, I know that 5 is made up of 3 and 2, or 1 and 4.
I can solve simple addition and subtraction problems within 5 without needing to use manipulatives or my fingers.

CC Approaching:
I can add two small groups of objects together without needing to physically manipulate them.
I can subtract small groups of objects from a larger group by physically taking them away.
I can use my fingers to help me add and subtract within 5.

CC Emerging:
I can count objects up to 5.
I can recognize and name numerals 0-5.
I can add two small groups of objects together, but I need to physically manipulate them to do so.

standards.domainName: Number and Operations in Base Ten
standards.clusterText: Work with numbers 11–19 to gain foundations for place value.
standards.text: Compose and decompose numbers from 11 to 19 into ten ones and some further ones, e.g., by using objects or drawings, and record each composition or decomposition by a drawing or equation (e.g., 18 = 10 + 8); understand that these numbers are composed of ten ones and one, two, three, four, five, six, seven, eight, or nine ones.

wi.text: Compose and decompose numbers from 11 to 19 into ten ones and some further ones, e.g., by using objects or drawings, and record each composition or decomposition by a drawing or numbers; understand that these numbers are composed of ten ones and one, two, three, four, five, six, seven, eight, or nine ones.
wi.levelDescriptors:
CC Advanced:
I can use objects, drawings, or numbers to show that 12 is made up of 10 and 2. I can also explain how this helps me understand other math concepts, such as place value and addition. I can also use this understanding to solve real-life problems, such as figuring out how much money I need to buy something if I have $10 and the item costs $12.

CC At Target:
I can use objects, drawings, or numbers to show that 12 is made up of 10 and 2. I understand that all numbers from 11 to 19 are made up of 10 ones and some further ones.

CC Approaching:
I can use objects or drawings to show that 12 is made up of 10 and 2, but I sometimes forget to show the 10 ones separately.

CC Emerging:
I can count objects to find the total number, but I don't understand that numbers like 12 are made up of 10 and 2.

standards.clusterText: Describe and compare measurable attributes.
standards.text: Describe measurable attributes of objects, such as length or weight. Describe several measurable attributes of a single object.

wi.text: Describe measurable attributes of objects, such as length or weight. Describe several measurable attributes of a single object.
wi.levelDescriptors:
CC Advanced:
I can: Describe several measurable attributes of a single object and use this information to solve real-world problems.
Example: A student wants to wrap a gift box that is 12 inches long, 8 inches wide, and 5 inches tall. They measure the wrapping paper and determine they need a piece that is at least 30 inches long and 20 inches wide to cover the box completely. They also calculate the amount of ribbon needed to tie a bow around the box based on its circumference.

CC At Target:
I can: Describe several measurable attributes of a single object, using appropriate vocabulary for length, weight, capacity, and other measurable features.
Example: A student picks up a book and says, "This book is about 10 inches long, 8 inches wide, and 2 inches thick. It weighs about 2 pounds and has 200 pages."

CC Approaching:
I can: Identify two measurable attributes of an object, such as its size and color.
Example: A student holds up a small blue cube and says, "It's small and blue."

CC Emerging:
I can: Identify one measurable attribute of an object, such as its color or shape.
Example: A student points to a red ball and says, "It's red!"

standards.clusterText: Describe and compare measurable attributes.
standards.text: Directly compare two objects with a measurable attribute in common, to see which object has “more of”/“less of” the attribute, and describe the difference. For example, directly compare the heights of two children and describe one child as taller/shorter.

wi.text: Directly compare two objects with a measurable attribute in common, to see which object has "more of" / "less of" the attribute and describe the difference. For example, directly compare the heights of two children and describe one child as taller/shorter.
wi.levelDescriptors:
CC Advanced:
I can directly compare two objects with a measurable attribute and explain the real-world implications of the difference.
I can use multiple units of measurement to compare the objects, converting between units as needed.
I can create a visual representation of the comparison, such as a graph or chart.
I can use my understanding of measurement and comparison to solve real-world problems, such as determining how much fabric is needed to make a dress or how much water to fill a pool.

CC At Target:
I can directly compare two objects with a measurable attribute and describe one object as having "more of" or "less of" the attribute.
I can use standard units of measurement to quantify the difference between the objects, such as inches or centimeters.
I can use precise language to describe the difference, such as "5 inches taller" or "2 centimeters shorter."
I can explain my reasoning for choosing the object with more or less of the attribute.

CC Approaching:
I can compare two objects with a measurable attribute and state which object has more or less of the attribute.
I can use comparative language to describe the difference, such as "longer" or "shorter."
I can use non-standard units of measurement to compare the objects, such as hand spans or footsteps.

CC Emerging:
I can identify that two objects have a measurable attribute in common, such as color or size.
I can use basic vocabulary to describe the attribute, such as "big" or "small."

standards.clusterText: Classify objects and count the number of objects in each category.
standards.text: Classify objects into given categories; count the numbers of objects in each category and sort the categories by count.

wi.text: Classify objects into given categories; count the numbers of objects in each category and sort the categories by count. Limit category counts to be less than or equal to 10.
wi.levelDescriptors:
CC Advanced:
I can sort objects into complex categories based on multiple attributes, like "round fruits" and "red vehicles."
I can count objects beyond 10 and use tally marks to keep track.
I can create graphs and charts to represent the data I collected from counting and sorting objects.
I can use my sorting and counting skills to solve real-life problems, like figuring out how many of each type of fruit I need to buy for a fruit salad.

CC At Target:
I can sort objects into specific categories like "fruits," "vegetables," and "animals."
I can count the number of objects in each category up to 10 and compare the quantities.
I can sort the categories by the number of objects in each, starting with the category with the most objects and ending with the category with the least.

CC Approaching:
I can sort objects into broad categories like "toys" and "clothes."
I can count objects up to 10, but I sometimes lose track or make mistakes.

CC Emerging:
I can sort objects by color, but I have difficulty putting them into specific categories like "fruits" or "vehicles."
I can count objects up to 5, but I struggle to keep track of larger quantities.

standards.clusterText: Identify and describe shapes (squares, circles, triangles, rectangles, hexagons, cubes, cones, cylinders, and spheres).
standards.text: Describe objects in the environment using names of shapes, and describe the relative positions of these objects using terms such as above, below, beside, in front of, behind, and next to.

wi.text: Describe objects in the environment using names of shapes and describe the relative positions of these objects using terms such as above, below, beside, in front of, behind, and next to.
wi.levelDescriptors:
CC Advanced:
I can identify and describe the properties of more complex shapes, such as pentagons, hexagons, and trapezoids.
I can use precise language to describe the relative positions of objects, including using multiple terms to describe the position of an object relative to another object.
I can apply my understanding of shapes and positions to solve problems in real-life situations, such as designing a layout for a room or navigating through a maze.

CC At Target:
I can identify and name various shapes, including triangles, rectangles, squares, circles, and ovals.
I can describe the relative positions of objects using terms like "above," "below," "beside," "in front of," "behind," and "next to."
I can use these terms accurately and consistently in different contexts.

CC Approaching:
I can identify most basic shapes like triangles, rectangles, and circles.
I can describe the position of an object using simple terms like "on top" or "underneath."
I can use some positional terms like "above" and "below" correctly.

CC Emerging:
I can identify some basic shapes like circles and squares.
I can point to objects and say they are "big" or "small."

standards.clusterText: Identify and describe shapes (squares, circles, triangles, rectangles, hexagons, cubes, cones, cylinders, and spheres).
standards.text: Correctly name shapes regardless of their orientations or overall size.

wi.text: Correctly name shapes regardless of their orientations or overall size.
wi.levelDescriptors:
CC Advanced:
I can not only name all common 2D and 3D shapes, but I can also describe their attributes (e.g., number of sides, corners, faces).
I can identify and name shapes in real-world objects and environments (e.g., the window is a rectangle, the ball is a sphere).
I can use my knowledge of shapes to solve problems, such as creating patterns or building structures.

CC At Target:
I can confidently name all common 2D shapes (circle, square, triangle, rectangle, pentagon, hexagon, octagon) regardless of their orientation or size.
I can identify and name some 3D shapes (sphere, cube, cone, cylinder) with minimal assistance.

CC Approaching:
I can name most common shapes like circles, squares, triangles, and rectangles, regardless of their orientation.
I can identify and name some less common shapes like ovals, hexagons, and stars, but I may need reminders or prompts.

CC Emerging:
I can sometimes name common shapes like circles and squares when they are presented in their standard orientation and size.
I can identify some shapes with assistance, but I struggle to name them independently.

standards.clusterText: Identify and describe shapes (squares, circles, triangles, rectangles, hexagons, cubes, cones, cylinders, and spheres).
standards.text: Identify shapes as two-dimensional (lying in a plane, “flat”) or three-dimensional (“solid”).

wi.text: Identify shapes as two-dimensional (lying in a plane, "flat") or three- dimensional ("solid").
wi.levelDescriptors:
CC Advanced:
I can identify and describe the properties of more complex shapes, like pentagons, pyramids, and prisms.
I can draw and build models of both flat and solid shapes.
I can use my understanding of flat and solid shapes to solve real-world problems, such as designing a box to hold a certain amount of objects.

CC At Target:
I can identify all common flat shapes, like circles, squares, triangles, and rectangles, and all common solid shapes, like spheres, cubes, cylinders, and cones.
I can explain the difference between flat and solid shapes using my own words.
I can sort objects by whether they are flat or solid.

CC Approaching:
I can identify some flat shapes, like circles and squares, and some solid shapes, like spheres and cubes.
I can tell the difference between some flat and solid shapes by looking at them, but I might not be able to explain the difference.

CC Emerging:
I can identify some familiar shapes, like circles and squares, but I don't know if they are flat or solid.
I can sort objects by color or size, but I don't understand the difference between flat and solid shapes.

standards.clusterText: Analyze, compare, create, and compose shapes.
standards.text: Analyze and compare two- and three-dimensional shapes, in different sizes and orientations, using informal language to describe their similarities, differences, parts (e.g., number of sides and vertices/“corners”) and other attributes (e.g., having sides of equal length).

wi.text: Analyze and compare two- and three-dimensional shapes, in different sizes and orientations, using informal language to describe their similarities, differences, parts (e.g., number of sides and vertices/"corners") and other attributes (e.g., having sides of equal length).
wi.levelDescriptors:
CC Advanced:
I can compare and contrast 2D and 3D shapes, using precise mathematical vocabulary.
I can explain how the properties of 2D and 3D shapes affect their real-world applications.
I can create my own 2D and 3D shapes with specific properties.

CC At Target:
I can analyze 2D and 3D shapes, using informal language to describe their similarities and differences.
I can identify the parts of 2D and 3D shapes, such as the number of sides, vertices, and faces.
I can describe other attributes of 2D and 3D shapes, such as whether they have sides of equal length or parallel sides.

CC Approaching:
I can describe the basic features of 2D shapes, such as the number of sides and corners.
I can compare two 2D shapes and identify some similarities and differences.

CC Emerging:
I can identify basic shapes like circles and squares.
I can sort shapes by color or size.

standards.clusterText: Analyze, compare, create, and compose shapes.

wi.text: Compose two-dimensional shapes (rectangles, squares, trapezoids, triangles, half-circles, and quarter- circles) or three-dimensional shapes (cubes, right rectangular prisms, right circular cones, and right circular cylinders) to create a composite shape, and compose new shapes from the composite shape. Student use of formal names such as "right rectangular prism" is not expected.
wi.levelDescriptors:
CC Advanced:
 I can use addition to understand and solve subtraction problems with unknown numbers.
 
CC At Target:
 I can understand subtraction as finding an unknown addend.
 
CC Approaching:
 I can use addition to help find the missing number in a subtraction problem.

CC Emerging:
I can put simple shapes together, like two triangles to make a square, with help (e.g., "With support, I used two triangles to make a square").
I can recognize a new shape made from smaller shapes with guidance.

standards.clusterText: Reason with shapes and their attributes.
standards.text: Partition circles and rectangles into two and four equal shares, describe the shares using the words halves, fourths, and quarters, and use the phrases half of, fourth of, and quarter of. Describe the whole as two of, or four of the shares. Understand for these examples that decomposing into more equal shares creates smaller shares.

wi.text: Partition circles and rectangles into two and four equal shares, describe and count the shares using the words halves and fourths, and use the phrases half of and fourth of the whole. Describe the whole as being two of the shares, or four of the shares. Understand for these examples that decomposing into more equal shares creates smaller shares.
wi.levelDescriptors:
CC Advanced:
 I can use addition to understand and solve subtraction problems with unknown numbers.

 CC At Target:
 I can understand subtraction as finding an unknown addend.
 
CC Approaching:
 I can use addition to help find the missing number in a subtraction problem.

CC Emerging:
I can divide a circle or rectangle into two equal parts and call each part a half, with help (e.g., "With help, I split a circle into two halves").
I can begin to understand that more equal parts make smaller shares, with guidance (e.g., "With support, I know that four parts are smaller than two parts").

standards.clusterText: Represent and solve problems involving addition and subtraction.
standards.text: Use addition and subtraction within 100 to solve one- and two-step word problems involving situations of adding to, taking from, putting together, taking apart, and comparing, with unknowns in all positions, e.g., by using drawings and equations with a symbol for the unknown number to represent the problem.

wi.text: Use addition and subtraction within 100 to solve one- and two-step word problems involving situations of adding to, taking from, putting together, taking apart, and comparing, with unknowns in all positions, e.g., by using drawings and equations with a symbol for the unknown number to represent the problem. See Appendix, Table 1 for specific problem situations and category information.
wi.levelDescriptors:
CC Advanced: 
I can use addition and subtraction within 100 to solve multi-step word problems.
I can write equations to represent multi-step word problems.
I can explain my thinking when solving multi-step word problems.
Example: I have $20. I want to buy a toy car that costs $12 and a toy airplane that costs $5. Do I have enough money to buy both toys?I can write the equation 20 - 12 - 5 = ___.I can explain that I need to subtract the cost of the car and the cost of the airplane from my total amount of money. I have $3 left, so I do not have enough money to buy both toys.

CC At Target:
I can use addition and subtraction within 100 to solve one- and two-step word problems.
I can identify the unknown in a one- or two-step word problem.
I can use drawings and equations with a symbol for the unknown number to represent the problem.
Example: There are 25 birds in a tree. 10 birds fly away. Then, 5 more birds come to the tree. How many birds are in the tree now?I can write the equation 25 - 10 + 5 = ___.I can draw 25 circles, cross out 10 circles, and then draw 5 more circles. There are 20 circles left, so there are 20 birds in the tree now.

CC Approaching:
I can use addition and subtraction within 100 to solve simple word problems.
I can identify the unknown in a simple word problem.
I can use drawings to help me solve simple word problems.
Example: I have 10 cookies. I eat 3 cookies. How many cookies do I have left?I can draw 10 circles and then cross out 3 circles. I have 7 circles left, so I have 7 cookies left.

CC Emerging:
I can add and subtract within 10.
I can identify the parts of a simple addition or subtraction problem.
I can use objects to help me solve simple addition and subtraction problems.
Example:I can count 5 apples and then add 3 more apples. I now have 8 apples.

standards.clusterText: Add and subtract within 20.
standards.text: Fluently add and subtract within 20 using mental strategies. By end of Grade 2, know from memory all sums of two one-digit numbers.

wi.text: Flexibly and efficiently add and subtract within 20 using multiple mental strategies which may include counting on; making ten; decomposing a number leading to a ten; using the relationship between addition and subtraction (e.g., knowing that 8 + 4 = 12, one knows 12 - 8 = 4); and creating equivalent but easier or known sums (e.g., adding 6 + 7 by creating the known equivalent 6 + 6 + 1 = 12 + 1 = 13).
wi.levelDescriptors:
CC Advanced: 
I can efficiently solve addition and subtraction problems within 20 using mental strategies, even when the problems involve larger numbers or decimals.
I can explain my thinking and the strategies I used to solve problems.
I can create and solve my own word problems involving addition and subtraction within 20. 

CC At Target:
I can flexibly use multiple mental strategies to add and subtract within 20, including counting on, making ten, and using known facts.
I can quickly and accurately recall all sums of two one-digit numbers.
I can apply my addition and subtraction skills to solve real-world problems involving small numbers.
ex. A student adds 14 + 6 by making a ten with 14: 14 + 6 = (10 + 4) + 6 = 10 + (4 + 6) = 10 + 10 = 20.

CC Approaching:
I can use counting on to add numbers within 20.
I can sometimes use making ten to add numbers within 20.
I can recall most sums of two one-digit numbers. ex, A student adds 8 + 7 by counting on from 8: 9, 10, 11, 12, 13, 14, 15.

CC Emerging:
I can add and subtract some numbers within 10 using my fingers or counting objects.
I can sometimes recall the sum of two small numbers without counting. ex. A student uses their fingers to count 5 + 3 by physically counting five fingers and then adding three more.

standards.clusterText: Work with equal groups of objects to gain foundations for multiplication.
standards.text: Determine whether a group of objects (up to 20) has an odd or even number of members, e.g., by pairing objects or counting them by 2s; write an equation to express an even number as a sum of two equal addends.

wi.text: Determine whether a group of objects (up to 20) has an odd or even number of members, e.g., by pairing objects or counting them by 2s; write an equation to express an even number as a sum of two equal addends.
wi.levelDescriptors:
CC Advanced: 
I can quickly identify if a large group of objects has an odd or even number of members, even if they are scattered or difficult to count individually.
I can explain different strategies for determining if a number is odd or even, such as looking for patterns in the digits or using divisibility rules.
I can use my understanding of odd and even numbers to solve real-world problems, such as figuring out how many people can be equally divided into groups of 2 or how many pieces of candy I need to buy so that everyone gets an even number.
I can create my own equations to represent even numbers as sums of two equal addends, andI can explain why my equations work.

CC At Target:
I can always identify if a group of objects (up to 20) has an odd or even number of members by pairing them up or counting them by 2s.
I can explain why counting by 2s helps me find even numbers.
I can write an equation to show any even number as a sum of two equal addends.

CC Approaching:
I can usually identify if a small group of objects (up to 10) has an odd or even number of members by pairing them up.
I can sometimes count objects by 2s, but I still make mistakes.
I can sometimes write an equation to show an even number as a sum of two equal addends, but I need help figuring out what the addends are.

CC Emerging:
I can sometimes identify if a group of objects has an odd or even number of members by looking at them, butI can't explain how I know.
I can count objects by 1s, but I don't understand how counting by 2s helps me find even numbers.

standards.clusterText: Work with equal groups of objects to gain foundations for multiplication.
standards.text: Use addition to find the total number of objects arranged in rectangular arrays with up to 5 rows and up to 5 columns; write an equation to express the total as a sum of equal addends.

wi.text: Use addition to find the total number of objects arranged in rectangular arrays with up to 5 rows and up to 5 columns; write an equation to express the total as a sum of equal addends.
wi.levelDescriptors:
CC Advanced: 
I can use the properties of addition, such as the commutative and associative properties, to solve addition problems involving rectangular arrays more efficiently.
I can apply my understanding of addition with rectangular arrays to solve real-world problems, such as calculating the total number of chairs needed for a classroom with a certain number of rows and columns.
I can create and solve my own problems involving addition with rectangular arrays.

CC At Target:
I can count the total number of objects in a rectangular array with up to 5 rows and 5 columns by skip counting or grouping objects.
I can write an addition equation with 5 or more addends to represent the total number of objects in a rectangular array.
I can explain how the rows and columns of a rectangular array relate to the addends in the addition equation.

CC Approaching:
I can count the total number of objects in a rectangular array with up to 4 rows and 4 columns by skip counting or grouping objects.
I can write an addition equation with 4 or 5 addends to represent the total number of objects in a rectangular array.

CC Emerging:
I can count the total number of objects in a rectangular array with up to 3 rows and 3 columns by counting each object individually.
I can write an addition equation with 2 or 3 addends to represent the total number of objects in a rectangular array.

standards.domainName: Number and Operations in Base Ten
standards.clusterText: Understand place value.
standards.text: Understand that the three digits of a three-digit number represent amounts of hundreds, tens, and ones; e.g., 706 equals 7 hundreds, 0 tens, and 6 ones. Understand the following as special cases:

wi.text: Understand that the three digits of a three-digit number represent amounts of hundreds, tens, and ones; e.g., 706 equals 7 hundreds, 0 tens, and 6 ones. Understand the following as special cases: a. 100 can be thought of as a bundle of ten tens -- called a "hundred". b. The numbers 100, 200, 300, 400, 500, 600, 700, 800, 900 refer to one, two, three, four, five, six, seven, eight, or nine hundreds (and 0 tens and 0 ones).
wi.levelDescriptors:
CC Advanced: 
I can use place value to compare and order three-digit numbers.
I can solve addition and subtraction problems with three-digit numbers.
I can explain how place value is used in real-life situations, such as counting money or measuring distances.
I can use place value to estimate the answer to a problem.

CC At Target:
I can understand that the three digits of a three-digit number represent amounts of hundreds, tens, and ones.
I can explain that 706 equals 7 hundreds, 0 tens, and 6 ones.
I can understand that 100 can be thought of as a bundle of ten tens, called a "hundred."
I can identify the numbers 100, 200, 300, 400, 500, 600, 700, 800, and 900 as one, two, three, four, five, six, seven, eight, or nine hundreds (and 0 tens and 0 ones).

CC Approaching:
I can explain that the digits in a three-digit number represent hundreds, tens, and ones.
I can use place value blocks to represent a three-digit number.
I can write the number of hundreds, tens, and ones for a given three-digit number.

CC Emerging:
I can identify the digits in a three-digit number.
I can group tens together to make a bundle of ten.

standards.domainName: Number and Operations in Base Ten
standards.clusterText: Understand place value.
standards.text: 100 can be thought of as a bundle of ten tens — called a “hundred.”

standards.domainName: Number and Operations in Base Ten
standards.clusterText: Understand place value.
standards.text: The numbers 100, 200, 300, 400, 500, 600, 700, 800, 900 refer to one, two, three, four, five, six, seven, eight, or nine hundreds (and 0 tens and 0 ones).

standards.domainName: Number and Operations in Base Ten
standards.clusterText: Understand place value.
standards.text: Count within 1000; skip-count by 5s, 10s, and 100s.

wi.text: Count within 1000; skip-count by 5s, 10s, and 100s.
wi.levelDescriptors:
CC Advanced: 
I can count objects beyond 1000.
I can identify and order large numbers.
I can skip-count by 5s, 10s, and 100s to solve problems.
I can apply skip-counting to real-life situations, such as counting the cost of items at the store or figuring out how many steps I take in a day.

CC At Target:
I can count objects up to 1000.
I can identify any number up to 1000.
I can skip-count by 5s, 10s, and 100s independently.

CC Approaching:
I can count objects up to 100.
I can identify most numbers up to 1000.
I can skip-count by 5s and 10s with some support.

CC Emerging:
I can count objects up to 20.
I can identify some numbers up to 100.
I can skip-count by 2s with some support.

standards.domainName: Number and Operations in Base Ten
standards.clusterText: Understand place value.
standards.text: Read and write numbers to 1000 using base-ten numerals, number names, and expanded form.

wi.text: Read and write numbers to 1000 using base-ten numerals, number names, and expanded form.
wi.levelDescriptors:
CC Advanced: 
I can read and write numbers larger than 1000.
I can use my understanding of place value to solve real-world problems involving large numbers (e.g., calculating the distance between two cities).
I can explain the concept of decimals and use them to represent parts of a whole.

CC At Target:
I can read and write numbers to 1000 using base-ten numerals, number names, and expanded form.
I can explain the value of each digit in a three-digit number (e.g., 345 = 3 hundreds + 4 tens + 5 ones).
I can use place value understanding to compare and order numbers to 1000.

CC Approaching:
I can write numbers to 100 using base-ten numerals.
I can read and write most number names up to 100.
I can begin to understand the concept of place value.

CC Emerging:
I can write numbers to 20 using base-ten numerals.
I can recognize some number names up to 100.

standards.domainName: Number and Operations in Base Ten
standards.clusterText: Understand place value.
standards.text: Compare two three-digit numbers based on meanings of the hundreds, tens, and ones digits, using >, =, and < symbols to record the results of comparisons.

wi.text: Compare two three-digit numbers based on meanings of the hundreds, tens, and ones digits, and describe the result of the comparison using words and symbols ( >, =, and < ).
wi.levelDescriptors:
CC Advanced: 
I can compare two three-digit numbers and explain which number is closest to a given target number.
I can use my understanding of place value to estimate the sum or difference of two three-digit numbers without using a calculator.
I can apply my knowledge of comparing three-digit numbers to real-life situations, such as comparing the populations of two cities or the heights of two buildings.

CC At Target:
I can compare two three-digit numbers based on the meanings of the hundreds, tens, and ones digits.
I can use the symbols >, =, and < to show which number is greater, equal to, or smaller than the other.
I can explain my reasoning using words like "because it has more hundreds," "because it has fewer tens," or "because they have the same hundreds and tens but different ones."

CC Approaching:
I can compare two three-digit numbers by looking at the hundreds and tens digits.
I can use the symbols >, =, and < to show which number is greater or smaller most of the time.
I can explain why one number is greater or smaller than another using words like "more" or "less."

CC Emerging:
I can compare two three-digit numbers by looking only at the first digit.
I can sometimes use the symbols >, =, and < to show which number is greater or smaller.

standards.domainName: Number and Operations in Base Ten
standards.clusterText: Use place value understanding and properties of operations to add and subtract.
standards.text: Fluently add and subtract within 100 using strategies based on place value, properties of operations, and/or the relationship between addition and subtraction.

wi.text: Flexibly and efficiently add and subtract within 100 using strategies based on place value, properties of operations, and/or the relationship between addition and subtraction. In Grade 2, subtraction with decomposition is an exception and may include drawings/representations.
wi.levelDescriptors:
CC Advanced: 
I can add and subtract three-digit numbers using mental math strategies based on place value, properties of operations, and/or the relationship between addition and subtraction.
I can apply my understanding of addition and subtraction to real-life situations, such as calculating the total cost of items at a store or figuring out how much change I will receive.
I can explain my reasoning clearly and concisely when solving addition and subtraction problems.

CC At Target:
I can add and subtract two-digit numbers using mental math strategies based on place value, properties of operations, and/or the relationship between addition and subtraction.
I can explain my thinking when adding and subtracting two-digit numbers.
I can solve word problems involving addition and subtraction within 100.

CC Approaching:
I can add and subtract two-digit numbers using manipulatives or drawings.
I can add and subtract two-digit numbers by decomposing one of the numbers into tens and ones.
I can identify the larger number in a subtraction problem and explain why it is the larger number.

CC Emerging:
I can add and subtract single-digit numbers using manipulatives or counting strategies.
I can add and subtract two-digit numbers by counting on or back from one of the numbers.
I can sometimes identify the larger number in a subtraction problem.

standards.domainName: Number and Operations in Base Ten
standards.clusterText: Use place value understanding and properties of operations to add and subtract.
standards.text: Add up to four two-digit numbers using strategies based on place value and properties of operations.

wi.text: Add up to four two-digit numbers using strategies based on place value and properties of operations.
wi.levelDescriptors:
CC Advanced: 
I can add up to four two-digit numbers together and apply this skill to real-life situations. For example,I can calculate the total cost of four items at the grocery store or figure out how many minutes it will take me to get to school if I walk for 15 minutes, ride my bike for 20 minutes, and take the bus for 10 minutes.

CC At Target:
I can add up to four two-digit numbers together using different strategies, such as place value, mental math, or decomposing numbers.I can explain my thinking and show my work.

CC Approaching:
I can add three two-digit numbers together by lining them up by place value and adding each place value column separately.

CC Emerging:
I can add two two-digit numbers together using my fingers or by counting objects.

standards.domainName: Number and Operations in Base Ten
standards.clusterText: Use place value understanding and properties of operations to add and subtract.
standards.text: Add and subtract within 1000, using concrete models or drawings and strategies based on place value, properties of operations, and/or the relationship between addition and subtraction; relate the strategy to a written method. Understand that in adding or subtracting three-digit numbers, one adds or subtracts hundreds and hundreds, tens and tens, ones and ones; and sometimes it is necessary to compose or decompose tens or hundreds.

wi.text: Add and subtract within 1000, using concrete models or drawings and strategies based on place value, properties of operations, and/or the relationship between addition and subtraction; relate the strategy to a written method. Understand that in adding or subtracting three-digit numbers, one adds or subtracts hundreds and hundreds, tens and tens, ones and ones; and sometimes it is necessary to compose or decompose tens or hundreds.
wi.levelDescriptors:
CC Advanced: 
I can apply my understanding of place value and addition/subtraction to solve real-world problems involving money, time, or measurement.
I can explain my thinking clearly and use different strategies to solve problems efficiently.
I can check my work and identify and correct any errors.
I can use my knowledge of addition and subtraction to estimate sums and differences and explain my reasoning.
I can explore and explain the properties of operations, such as the commutative and associative properties, and use these properties to solve problems more efficiently.

CC At Target:
I can add and subtract three-digit numbers using concrete models or drawings and strategies based on place value.
I can explain the relationship between addition and subtraction and use this understanding to solve problems.
I can relate my addition and subtraction strategies to a written method, such as the standard algorithm.
I understand that in adding or subtracting three-digit numbers, I add or subtract hundreds and hundreds, tens and tens, ones and ones.
I know that sometimes it is necessary to compose or decompose tens or hundreds to solve a problem.

CC Approaching:
I can add and subtract three-digit numbers using manipulatives and drawings, but I sometimes make mistakes when regrouping.
I can explain the concept of place value and use it to add and subtract two-digit numbers, but I still need support when working with three-digit numbers.

CC Emerging:
I can add and subtract two-digit numbers using manipulatives, but I struggle to connect this to place value concepts.
I can add three-digit numbers by counting on from the larger number, but I don't understand the concept of composing and decomposing tens and hundreds.

standards.domainName: Number and Operations in Base Ten
standards.clusterText: Use place value understanding and properties of operations to add and subtract.
standards.text: Mentally add 10 or 100 to a given number 100–900, and mentally subtract 10 or 100 from a given number 100–900.

wi.text: Mentally add 10 or 100 to a given number 100 - 900, and mentally subtract 10 or 100 from a given number 100 - 900.
wi.levelDescriptors:
CC Advanced: 
I can mentally add or subtract multiples of 10 and 100 in different combinations to solve problems, like "If I add 30 and then subtract 70 from 540, what do I get?"
I can use mental math to estimate the cost of items at the grocery store or calculate the remaining time before an event based on the current time and duration.

CC At Target:
I can mentally add 10 or 100 to any number between 100 and 900, like 235 + 100 or 689 + 10.
I can mentally subtract 10 or 100 from any number between 100 and 900, like 876 - 10 or 452 - 100.

CC Approaching:
I can mentally add 10 to a two-digit number without using my fingers, like 47 + 10.
I can mentally subtract 100 from a three-digit number without using a number line, like 750 - 100.

CC Emerging:
I can count on my fingers to add 10 to a two-digit number, like 34 + 10.
I can use a number line to subtract 100 from a three-digit number, like 500 - 100.

standards.domainName: Number and Operations in Base Ten
standards.clusterText: Use place value understanding and properties of operations to add and subtract.
standards.text: Explain why addition and subtraction strategies work, using place value and the properties of operations.

wi.text: Explain why addition and subtraction strategies work, using place value and the properties of operations. These explanations may be supported by drawings or objects.
wi.levelDescriptors:
CC Advanced: 
I can explain why addition and subtraction strategies work using place value and the properties of operations in a clear and concise way.
I can use my understanding of place value and the properties of operations to solve real-world problems.
I can create my own addition and subtraction strategies based on my understanding of place value and the properties of operations.

CC At Target:
I can explain why addition and subtraction strategies work using place value and the properties of operations.
I can use drawings, objects, and manipulatives to support my explanations.
I can explain how the commutative, associative, and distributive properties of addition and multiplication relate to addition and subtraction strategies.

CC Approaching:
I can explain how place value helps me add and subtract two-digit numbers, but I still need help understanding how the properties of operations relate to these strategies.
I can use drawings and objects to explain why some addition and subtraction strategies work, but my explanations are not always clear or complete.

CC Emerging:
I can explain addition and subtraction strategies using simple drawings, but I have difficulty connecting them to place value.
I can identify some properties of operations, such as the commutative property of addition, butI cannot explain how they relate to addition and subtraction strategies.

standards.clusterText: Measure and estimate lengths in standard units.
standards.text: Measure the length of an object by selecting and using appropriate tools such as rulers, yardsticks, meter sticks, and measuring tapes.

wi.text: Measure the length of an object by selecting and using appropriate tools such as rulers, yardsticks, meter sticks, and measuring tapes.
wi.levelDescriptors:
CC Advanced: 
I can explain why I chose a specific tool to measure the length of an object.
I can use my measurement skills to solve real-world problems, such as figuring out how much fabric I need to make a curtain or how much yarn I need to knit a scarf.
I can convert between different units of measurement (e.g., inches to feet, centimeters to meters).

CC At Target:
I can choose the right tool (ruler, yardstick, meter stick, or measuring tape) to measure the length of an object based on its size.
I can line up the tool with the ends of the object and read the numbers correctly to measure its length.
I can record the length of the object using appropriate units (inches, feet, yards, centimeters, meters).

CC Approaching:
I can line up a ruler with the end of an object, but I sometimes have trouble reading the numbers correctly.
I can use a ruler to measure the length of an object, but I might not choose the right tool for the job (e.g., using a ruler to measure a long piece of fabric).

CC Emerging:
I can hold a ruler next to an object, but I don't know how to line it up with the ends of the object.
I can try to measure with a ruler, but I don't understand how to read the numbers on it.

standards.clusterText: Measure and estimate lengths in standard units.
standards.text: Measure the length of an object twice, using length units of different lengths for the two measurements; describe how the two measurements relate to the size of the unit chosen.

wi.text: Measure the length of an object twice, using length units of different lengths for the two measurements; describe how the two measurements relate to the size of the unit chosen.
wi.levelDescriptors:
CC Advanced: 
I can measure the length of an object using different units of measurement and convert between them.
I can explain the relationship between different units of measurement (e.g., inches, feet, centimeters, meters).
I can use my understanding of measurement to solve real-world problems.
For example,I can determine how much fabric I need to buy to make a curtain, knowing the length of the window in feet and the fabric is sold by the yard.

CC At Target:
I can measure the length of an object twice, using different units of measurement for each measurement.
I can identify the unit of measurement used for each measurement.
I can compare the two measurements and describe how the size of the unit chosen affects the measurement.
I can explain that using a smaller unit will result in a larger measurement and vice versa.

CC Approaching:
I can measure the length of an object using a ruler and identify the unit of measurement.
I can compare two measurements of the same object using different units and recognize that the measurements will be different.
I can explain that a smaller unit will result in a larger measurement and vice versa. 

CC Emerging:
I can measure the length of an object using a ruler.
I can identify the length of an object as being longer or shorter than another object.

standards.clusterText: Measure and estimate lengths in standard units.
standards.text: Estimate lengths using units of inches, feet, centimeters, and meters.

wi.text: Estimate lengths using units of inches, feet, centimeters, and meters.
wi.levelDescriptors:
CC Advanced: 
I can use my knowledge of length to solve real-world problems, such as figuring out how much fabric I need to make a curtain or how much string I need to wrap a gift.
I can estimate the length of objects from a distance, using visual cues like the size of a person or the height of a building.
I can convert between different units of length (inches to feet, centimeters to meters, etc.).

CC At Target:
I can use rulers and measuring tapes to measure the length of objects to the nearest inch, foot, centimeter, or meter.
I can estimate the length of objects by comparing them to other objects with known lengths.
I can explain my reasoning for choosing a particular unit to estimate the length of an object.

CC Approaching:
I can use non-standard units, like hand spans or paperclips, to estimate the length of objects.
I can choose the most appropriate unit (inches, feet, centimeters, or meters) to estimate the length of an object.

CC Emerging:
I can guess the length of objects without using any measuring tools.
I can compare the lengths of two objects by holding them up to each other.

standards.clusterText: Measure and estimate lengths in standard units.
standards.text: Measure to determine how much longer one object is than another, expressing the length difference in terms of a standard length unit.

wi.text: Measure to determine how much longer one object is than another, expressing the length difference in terms of a standard-length unit.
wi.levelDescriptors:
CC Advanced: 
I can use a ruler to measure the lengths of two objects and calculate the difference in length as a fraction of the longer object's length.
I can use my knowledge of length measurement to solve real-world problems, such as determining how much longer a piece of string needs to be to wrap around a box.

CC At Target:
I can use a ruler to measure the lengths of two objects and find the exact difference in length.
I can express the length difference in terms of a standard-length unit (e.g., inches, centimeters).

CC Approaching:
I can use a ruler to measure the lengths of two objects and say which one is longer or shorter.
I can use a ruler to measure the lengths of two objects and estimate the difference in length.

CC Emerging:
I can compare the lengths of two objects by holding them end-to-end and saying which one is longer or shorter.
I can use non-standard units like hand-spans or pencils to measure the lengths of two objects and say which one is longer.

standards.clusterText: Relate addition and subtraction to length.
standards.text: Use addition and subtraction within 100 to solve word problems involving lengths that are given in the same units, e.g., by using drawings (such as drawings of rulers) and equations with a symbol for the unknown number to represent the problem.

wi.text: Use addition and subtraction within 100 to solve word problems involving lengths that are given in the same units, e.g., by using drawings (such as number lines) and equations with a symbol for the unknown number to represent the problem.
wi.levelDescriptors:
CC Advanced: 
I can add and subtract multi-digit numbers within 1000, using efficient strategies like regrouping or mental math.
I can create and solve my own word problems involving addition and subtraction within 1000, using real-life contexts and different units of measure for lengths.
I can explain my thinking and strategies clearly, using mathematical vocabulary and representations.

CC At Target:
I can add and subtract numbers within 100, using a variety of strategies like counting on, making ten, or using a number line.
I can use drawings and equations with a symbol for the unknown number to represent and solve word problems involving addition and subtraction within 100, where the lengths are given in the same units.

CC Approaching:
I can add and subtract numbers within 50, using manipulatives or mental math strategies.
I can use drawings and equations to represent simple word problems involving addition and subtraction within 50, but I may need some support interpreting the problem.

CC Emerging:
I can add and subtract numbers within 10, but I struggle with larger numbers.
I can use drawings to represent simple addition and subtraction problems, but I have difficulty connecting them to equations.

standards.clusterText: Relate addition and subtraction to length.
standards.text: Represent whole numbers as lengths from 0 on a number line diagram with equally spaced points corresponding to the numbers 0, 1, 2, ..., and represent whole-number sums and differences within 100 on a number line diagram.

wi.text: Represent whole numbers as lengths from 0 on a number line with equally spaced points corresponding to the numbers 0, 1, 2 ... and represent whole-number sums and differences within 100 on a number line.
wi.levelDescriptors:
CC Advanced: 
I can explain how the distance between points on the number line relates to the size of the numbers.
I can use the number line to solve addition and subtraction problems within 100.
I can create my own number line with different scales and use it to represent and solve problems involving larger numbers.
I can use the number line to estimate the sum or difference of two whole numbers that are close together, even if they are larger than 100.
I can use the number line to explain why some addition and subtraction problems have more than one possible answer.

CC At Target:
I can draw a number line with equally spaced points and label them with whole numbers from 0 to 10.
I can locate any whole number from 0 to 10 on the number line.
I can represent the sum or difference of two whole numbers within 100 by marking the starting point, the end point, and the sum or difference on the number line.

CC Approaching:
I can draw a number line with equally spaced points.
I can label some of the points on the number line with whole numbers.
I can estimate the location of a whole number on the number line.

CC Emerging:
I can draw a line and label the starting point as "0".
I can count objects and say how many there are.

standards.clusterText: Work with time and money.
standards.text: Tell and write time from analog and digital clocks to the nearest five minutes, using a.m. and p.m.

wi.text: Tell and write time from analog and digital clocks to the nearest five minutes, using a.m. and p.m.
wi.levelDescriptors:
CC Advanced:
I can solve word problems involving time (e.g., "The movie starts at 6:30 p.m. and is 2 hours long. What time will the movie end?").
I can use a schedule to plan my day, including activities and estimated times for each activity.
I can explain how time is measured and the relationship between seconds, minutes, and hours.
I can convert time between different units (e.g., minutes to hours, hours to days).                                                                                                                                                          

CC At Target: 
I can tell the time on an analog clock to the nearest five minutes.
I can tell the time on a digital clock to the nearest five minutes.
I can write the time using a.m. and p.m. for any time of day.
I can differentiate between a.m. and p.m. and explain when each is used.                                                                                                                                                                           

CC Approaching: 
I can tell the time on an analog clock to the nearest hour.
I can tell the time on a digital clock when the minutes are at the 30 mark (e.g., 10:30, 1:30).
I can write the time using a.m. and p.m. for simple times (e.g., 8:00 a.m., 5:00 p.m.).                                                                                                                                                  

CC Emerging : 
I can identify the hour hand on an analog clock.
I can tell the time on a digital clock when the minutes are at the 00 mark (e.g., 10:00, 2:00).

standards.clusterText: Work with time and money.
standards.text: Solve word problems involving dollar bills, quarters, dimes, nickels, and pennies, using $ and ¢ symbols appropriately. Example: If you have 2 dimes and 3 pennies, how many cents do you have?

wi.text: Solve word problems involving dollar bills, quarters, dimes, nickels, and pennies, using $ and ¢ symbols appropriately. Example: If you have 2 dimes and 3 pennies, how many cents do you have?
wi.levelDescriptors:
CC Advanced: 
I can solve real-life word problems involving money.I can figure out how much money I need to buy groceries, how much change I will get back from a purchase, or how much money I have saved after spending some money.
I can use mental math strategies to solve money problems.I can use my knowledge of coin values and place value to add and subtract money amounts in my head.
I can explain my thinking when solving money problems.I can tell you how I solved a problem and why I chose the strategy I used.
I can use technology to help me solve money problems.I can use a calculator or a spreadsheet to help me add and subtract money amounts.

CC At Target:
I can solve word problems involving dollar bills, quarters, dimes, nickels, and pennies.I can answer questions like "If I have 2 quarters, 3 dimes, and 5 pennies, how much money do I have?" or "I have $2.00. I want to buy a candy bar that costs $1.50. How much change will I get back?"
I can add and subtract coins and bills of different values.I can add a group of quarters and dimes and tell you the total value.I can also subtract a group of nickels from a dollar bill and tell you how much money is left.
I can use $ and ¢ symbols correctly and consistently.I can write the amount of money in a problem and in my answer using the correct symbols, like $3.75 or 25¢.

CC Approaching:
I can solve simple word problems involving coins.I can answer questions like "How many pennies are there in 25 cents?" or "How much money is 3 dimes and 2 pennies?"
I can add and subtract coins of the same value.I can add two groups of dimes or subtract 2 nickels from a group of 5 nickels and tell you the answer.
I can use $ and ¢ symbols correctly.I can write the amount of money in a problem using the correct symbols, like $1.25 or 50¢.

CC Emerging:
I can identify coins and bills.I can point to a penny, nickel, dime, quarter, and dollar bill and say their names.
I can count coins and bills.I can count a small group of coins and bills (up to 5) and tell you how much money there is in total.
I can add coins of the same value.I can put together two groups of pennies and tell you how many pennies there are in total.

standards.clusterText: Represent and interpret data.
standards.text: Generate measurement data by measuring lengths of several objects to the nearest whole unit, or by making repeated measurements of the same object. Show the measurements by making a line plot, where the horizontal scale is marked off in whole-number units.

wi.text: Generate measurement data by measuring lengths of several objects to the nearest whole unit, or by making repeated measurements of the same object. Show the measurements by making a line plot, where the horizontal scale is marked off in whole-number units.
wi.levelDescriptors:
CC Advanced: 
I can use a ruler to measure the length of objects to the nearest half-inch.
I can calculate the perimeter of simple shapes using my measurements.
I can use my measurements to create a scale drawing of a room in my house.
I can analyze my line plot to identify the most common object length and the range of lengths.
I can use my data to answer questions about the objects I measured, such as "Which object is the longest?" or "How many objects are longer than 5 inches?"

CC At Target:
I can use a ruler to measure the length of several objects to the nearest whole unit.
I can make repeated measurements of the same object to ensure accuracy.
I can create a line plot to show the lengths of different objects, marking the horizontal scale in whole-number units.

CC Approaching:
I can use a ruler to measure the length of objects to the nearest inch.
I can record my measurements using numbers.
I can create a simple chart to show the lengths of different objects.

CC Emerging:
I can use non-standard units (hand, foot) to measure the length of objects.
I can order objects by length without using any measuring tools.

standards.clusterText: Represent and interpret data.
standards.text: Draw a picture graph and a bar graph (with single-unit scale) to represent a data set with up to four categories. Solve simple put-together, take-apart, and compare problems using information presented in a bar graph.

wi.text: Draw a picture graph and a bar graph (with single-unit scale) to represent a data set with up to four categories. Solve simple put together, take-apart, and compare problems using information presented in a bar graph. See Appendix, Table 1 for specific problem situations.
wi.levelDescriptors:
CC Advanced: 
I can create a picture graph and a bar graph to represent a data set with more than four categories.
I can use the information from a bar graph to solve multi-step problems that require me to combine and compare data.
I can create my own bar graphs to represent data I have collected in real-life situations, such as the favorite colors of my classmates or the number of students who walk, bike, or take the bus to school.

CC At Target:
I can draw a picture graph and a bar graph (with single-unit scale) to represent a data set with up to four categories.
I can solve simple put-together, take-apart, and compare problems using information presented in a bar graph.

CC Approaching:
I can draw a picture graph with accurate data, but I have difficulty labeling the categories.
I can answer simple questions about the data in a bar graph, such as "Which category has the most?"

CC Emerging:
I can draw a picture graph, but it is inaccurate or incomplete.
I can identify the tallest bar in a bar graph, butI cannot answer questions about the data.

standards.clusterText: Reason with shapes and their attributes.
standards.text: Recognize and draw shapes having specified attributes, such as a given number of angles or a given number of equal faces. Identify triangles, quadrilaterals, pentagons, hexagons, and cubes.

wi.text: Recognize and draw shapes having specified attributes, such as a given number of angles or a given number of equal faces. Identify triangles, quadrilaterals, pentagons, hexagons, and cubes. Sizes are compared directly or visually, not compared by measuring.
wi.levelDescriptors:
CC Advanced: 
I can draw and identify shapes with different numbers of sides and angles, including more complex shapes like octagons and dodecahedrons.
I can explain the relationships between different shapes, such as how a square is a type of rectangle.
I can use my knowledge of shapes to solve real-world problems, such as designing a building or creating a pattern.
I can compare the sizes of different shapes using precise measurements and calculations.

CC At Target:
I can draw shapes with different numbers of sides and angles, like triangles, quadrilaterals, pentagons, and hexagons.
I can identify and name common shapes, including triangles, quadrilaterals, pentagons, hexagons, and cubes.
I can identify the specific attributes of these shapes, such as the number of sides, angles, and faces.
I can compare the sizes of different shapes directly or visually, using terms like "bigger," "smaller," "same size," and "equal."

CC Approaching:
I can draw shapes with different numbers of sides and identify them by name, like triangles and squares.
I can recognize most common shapes, like circles, squares, and triangles, and identify their specific attributes, like the number of sides and angles.
I can compare the sizes of different shapes visually, but I might not be able to use specific terms like "bigger" or "smaller."

CC Emerging:
I can draw shapes with different numbers of sides, but I might not be able to identify them by name.
I can recognize some common shapes, like circles and squares, but I might not be able to identify their specific attributes, like the number of sides or angles.

standards.clusterText: Reason with shapes and their attributes.
standards.text: Partition a rectangle into rows and columns of same-size squares and count to find the total number of them.

wi.text: Partition a rectangle into rows and columns of same-size squares and count to find the total number of them.
wi.levelDescriptors:
CC Advanced: 
I can cut a rectangle into equal rows and columns of squares and explain why it is important for the squares to be the same size.
I can use the area of the rectangle and the area of one square to find the total number of squares.
I can apply my understanding of partitioning rectangles to solve real-world problems, such as figuring out how many tiles I need to cover a floor.

CC At Target:
I can cut a rectangle into equal rows and columns of squares.
I can count the total number of squares by multiplying the number of rows by the number of columns.

CC Approaching:
I can cut a rectangle into rows and columns of squares, but the squares might not be perfectly the same size.
I can count the squares in one row or column, but I might have trouble counting all the rows and columns.

CC Emerging:
