I can use my understanding of multiplication to estimate products and check the reasonableness of my answers.

CC At Target:
I can multiply a whole number of up to four digits by a one-digit whole number using strategies based on place value and the properties of operations.
I can illustrate and explain the calculation by using equations, rectangular arrays, and/or area models.
I can multiply two two-digit numbers using strategies based on place value and the properties of operations.
I can illustrate and explain the calculation by using equations, rectangular arrays, and/or area models.

CC Approaching:
I can use place value blocks or drawings to represent the multiplication of a two-digit whole number by a one-digit whole number.
I can break down a two-digit whole number into tens and ones and multiply each part by a one-digit whole number.
I can use the distributive property to rewrite and solve multiplication problems.

CC Emerging:
I can skip count by a one-digit whole number to find the product of a small whole number and a one-digit whole number.
I can use repeated addition to find the product of a small whole number and a one-digit whole number.

standards.domainName: Number and Operations in Base Ten
standards.clusterText: Use place value understanding and properties of operations to perform multi-digit arithmetic.
standards.text: Find whole-number quotients and remainders with up to four-digit dividends and one-digit divisors, using strategies based on place value, the properties of operations, and/or the relationship between multiplication and division. Illustrate and explain the calculation by using equations, rectangular arrays, and/or area models.

wi.text: Find whole-number quotients and remainders with up to four-digit dividends and one-digit divisors, using strategies based on place value, the properties of operations, and/or the relationship between multiplication and division. Illustrate and explain the calculation by using equations, rectangular arrays, and/or area models.
wi.levelDescriptors:
CC Advanced:
I can solve multi-step word problems involving division of whole numbers.
I can apply division to real-life situations, such as calculating the number of equal groups that can be made from a given set of objects or determining the cost per item when buying multiple items.
I can explain my reasoning and strategies for solving division problems clearly and effectively.
I can use my understanding of division to estimate quotients and check the reasonableness of my answers.

CC At Target:
I can find whole-number quotients and remainders with up to four-digit dividends and one-digit divisors.
I can use strategies based on place value, the properties of operations, and/or the relationship between multiplication and division.
I can illustrate and explain the calculation by using equations, rectangular arrays, and/or area models.

CC Approaching:
I can use place value blocks or drawings to represent the division of a two-digit whole number by a one-digit divisor.
I can break down a two-digit whole number into tens and ones and divide each part by a one-digit divisor.
I can use the distributive property to rewrite and solve division problems.

CC Emerging:
I can skip count to find the quotient of a small whole number and a one-digit divisor.
I can use repeated subtraction to find the quotient of a small whole number and a one-digit divisor.

standards.clusterText: Extend understanding of fraction equivalence and ordering.
standards.text: Explain why a fraction a/b is equivalent to a fraction (n×a)/(n×b) by using visual fraction models, with attention to how the number and size of the parts differ even though the two fractions themselves are the same size. Use this principle to recognize and generate equivalent fractions.

wi.text: Understand fraction equivalence. Explain why a fraction is equivalent to another fraction by using visual fraction models (e.g., tape diagrams and number lines), with attention to how the number and the size of the parts differ even though the two fractions themselves are the same size. Understand and use a general principle to recognize and generate equivalent fractions that name the same amount.
levelDescriptors:
CC Advanced:
I can apply my understanding of fraction equivalence to solve real-world problems.
I can explain why a fraction is equivalent to another fraction using visual models, a general principle, and real-world examples.
I can use a general principle to recognize and generate equivalent fractions in complex situations.

CC At Target:
I can explain why a fraction is equivalent to another fraction using visual models and a general principle.
I can identify that fractions with the same numerator or denominator are equivalent and can explain why.
I can use a general principle to recognize and generate equivalent fractions.

CC Approaching:
I can explain why some fractions are equivalent using visual models.
I can identify that fractions with the same numerator or denominator are equivalent and can explain why.

CC Emerging:
I can recognize that some fractions represent the same amount as others.
I can identify that fractions with the same numerator or denominator are equivalent

CC Advanced:
I can explain why multiplying or dividing both the numerator and the denominator by the same number creates equivalent fractions and use this method to generate and check equivalent fractions (e.g., "I know that 2/3 and 4/6 are equivalent because I multiplied both parts of 2/3 by 2").
I can apply the general principle of equivalent fractions to solve real-world problems and explain my reasoning.

CC At Target:
I can recognize and create equivalent fractions by multiplying or dividing the numerator and denominator by the same number (e.g., "I multiplied 1/2 by 2/2 to make 2/4, so I know 1/2 is equivalent to 2/4").
I can use this general principle to show how fractions with different numerators and denominators can represent the same amount.

CC Approaching:
I can identify equivalent fractions by using multiplication or division with some guidance (e.g., "With help, I found that 3/4 is the same as 6/8 because I multiplied both 3 and 4 by 2").
I can start to understand that equivalent fractions name the same amount even if they look different.

CC Emerging:
I can begin to understand that fractions can represent the same amount when their parts are multiplied or divided by the same number, with support (e.g., "With guidance, I saw that 1/3 and 2/6 cover the same amount on a fraction bar").
I can try using simple examples to see how fractions like 1/2 and 2/4 name the same amount, with help.

standards.clusterText: Extend understanding of fraction equivalence and ordering.
standards.text: Compare two fractions with different numerators and different denominators, e.g., by creating common denominators or numerators, or by comparing to a benchmark fraction such as 1/2. Recognize that comparisons are valid only when the two fractions refer to the same whole. Record the results of comparisons with symbols >, =, or <, and justify the conclusions, e.g., by using a visual fraction model.

wi.text: Compare fractions with different numerators and different denominators while recognizing that comparisons are valid only when the fractions refer to the same whole. Justify the conclusions by using visual fraction models (e.g., tape diagrams and number lines) and by reasoning about the size of the fractions, using benchmark fractions (including whole numbers), or creating common denominators or numerators. Describe the result of the comparison using words and symbols ( >, =, and < ).
wi.levelDescriptors:
CC Advanced:
I can compare fractions with different numerators and denominators by using multiple strategies, including visual models, benchmark fractions, creating common denominators or numerators, and reasoning about the size of the fractions.
I can explain my reasoning clearly and concisely.
I can apply my understanding of comparing fractions to real-world situations. For example, I can compare the amount of juice in two different containers or the distance two runners have traveled.
I can use my understanding of comparing fractions to solve problems. For example, I can find the difference between two fractions or the sum of two fractions.

CC At Target:
I can compare fractions with different numerators and denominators by using visual models like fraction strips, number lines, and area models.
I can use benchmark fractions like halves, fourths, and thirds to estimate the size of fractions.
I can create common denominators or numerators to compare fractions.
I can explain my reasoning when comparing fractions using multiple strategies.
I can use the symbols >, =, and < to describe the results of my comparisons.

CC Approaching:
I can compare fractions with different numerators and denominators by using visual models like fraction strips or number lines.
I can use benchmark fractions like halves and fourths to estimate the size of fractions.

wi.text: Understand composing and decomposing fractions. a. Understand addition and subtraction of fractions as joining and separating parts referring to the same whole. Decompose a fraction into a sum of unit fractions and/or multiples of that unit fraction in more than one way, recording each decomposition by an equation. Justify decompositions with explanations, visual fraction models, or equations. For example: 3/8 = 1/8 + 1/8 + 1/8; 3/8 = 1/8 + 2/8; 2 1/8 = 1 + 1 + 1/8 = 8/8 + 8/8 + 1/8. Add and subtract fractions, including mixed numbers, with like denominators (e.g., 3/8 + 2/8) and related denominators (e.g., 1/2 +1/4, 1/3 + 1/6) by using visual fraction models (e.g., tape diagrams and number lines), properties of operations, and the relationship between addition and subtraction. Solve word problems involving addition and subtraction of fractions with like and related denominators, including mixed numbers, by using visual fraction models and equations to represent the problem. Students are not required to rename fractions in lowest terms nor use least common denominators.

wi.text: Apply and extend previous understandings of multiplication to multiply a whole number times a fraction. Understand a fraction as a group of unit fractions or as a multiple of a unit fraction. For example, 5/4 can be represented visually as 5 groups of ¼, as a sum of unit fractions ¼ + ¼ + ¼ + ¼ + ¼, or as a multiple of a unit fraction 5 x ¼. Represent a whole number times a non- unit fraction (e.g., 3 x 2/5) using visual fraction models and understand this as combining equal groups of the non-unit fraction (3 groups of 2/5) and as a collection of unit fractions (6 groups of 1/5), recognizing this product as 6/5. Solve word problems involving multiplication of a whole number times a fraction by using visual fraction models and equations to represent the problem. Understand a reasonable answer range when multiplying with fractions. For example, if each person at a party will eat 3/8 of a pound of roast beef, and there will be 5 people at the party, how many pounds of roast beef will be needed? Between what two whole numbers does your answer lie?

standards.text: Express a fraction with denominator 10 as an equivalent fraction with denominator 100, and use this technique to add two fractions with respective denominators 10 and 100. For example, express 3/10 as 30/100, and add 3/10 + 4/100 = 34/100.

wi.text: Recognize angles as geometric shapes that are formed wherever two rays share a common endpoint, and understand concepts of angle measurement: An angle is measured with reference to a circle with its center at the common endpoint of the rays, by considering the fraction of the circular arc between the points where the two rays intersect the circle. An angle that turns through n one-degree angles is said to have an angle measure of n degrees.

I can apply my knowledge of geometric shapes to solve real-world problems, such as measuring the area of a room or calculating the distance between two points.

CC At Target:
I can draw points, lines, line segments, rays, angles (right, acute, obtuse), and perpendicular and parallel lines.
I can identify these shapes in two-dimensional figures.

CC Approaching:
I can draw lines, line segments, and rays.
I can identify right angles in shapes.
I can identify parallel lines in pictures.

CC Emerging:
I can draw simple shapes like squares and circles.
I can identify some shapes like triangles and rectangles in pictures.

standards.clusterText: Draw and identify lines and angles, and classify shapes by properties of their lines and angles.
standards.text: Classify two-dimensional figures based on the presence or absence of parallel or perpendicular lines, or the presence or absence of angles of a specified size. Recognize right triangles as a category, and identify right triangles.

wi.text: Classify two-dimensional figures based on the presence or absence of parallel or perpendicular lines, or the presence or absence of angles of a specified size. Recognize right triangles as a category and identify right triangles.
wi.levelDescriptors:
CC Advanced:
I can classify and describe complex 2D figures, including those with multiple types of lines and angles.
I can use my knowledge of angles and lines to solve problems, such as finding missing angle measures or determining if two figures are congruent.
I can apply my understanding of right triangles to real-world situations, such as calculating the height of a building or the distance across a river.
I can explain the relationship between right triangles and other geometric concepts, such as Pythagorean theorem and trigonometry.
I can create my own 2D figures with specific properties, such as a quadrilateral with two pairs of parallel sides and four right angles (a rectangle).


CC At Target:
I can classify any 2D figure based on the presence or absence of parallel or perpendicular lines, or the presence or absence of angles of a specified size.
I can explain the difference between parallel and perpendicular lines and identify them in complex figures.
I can identify and measure angles using a protractor, including right angles and other specific angle sizes.
I can recognize and identify right triangles based on their properties, including a right angle and two acute angles.
I can explain why a triangle with a right angle is called a "right triangle."

CC Approaching:
I can identify most common 2D shapes, including triangles, squares, rectangles, and circles.
I can identify parallel and perpendicular lines in simple figures.
I can identify right angles in shapes and understand that they measure 90 degrees.
I can recognize some right triangles, but I may not be able to explain why they are right triangles.

CC Emerging:
I can identify some shapes, like circles and squares, but I have difficulty identifying shapes with more sides or complex features.
I can sometimes tell if lines are straight or curved, but I don't understand the difference between parallel and perpendicular lines.
I can recognize some angles as "big" or "small," but I don't know the specific names for different angle sizes.
I have seen triangles before, but I don't know what makes a triangle a "right triangle."

standards.clusterText: Draw and identify lines and angles, and classify shapes by properties of their lines and angles.
standards.text: Recognize a line of symmetry for a two-dimensional figure as a line across the figure such that the figure can be folded along the line into matching parts. Identify line-symmetric figures and draw lines of symmetry.

wi.text: Recognize a line of symmetry for a two- dimensional figure as a line across the figure such that the figure can be folded along the line into matching parts. Identify line- symmetric figures and draw lines of symmetry.
wi.levelDescriptors:
CC Advanced:
I can identify lines of symmetry for three-dimensional figures.
I can also use my understanding of line symmetry to create symmetrical designs and patterns.

CC At Target:
I can identify a line of symmetry for any two-dimensional figure.
I can also draw lines of symmetry for two-dimensional figures.

CC Approaching:
I can identify a line of symmetry for some figures, but I still have trouble with others, especially if the figure has multiple lines of symmetry.

CC Emerging:
I can identify a line that divides a figure in half, but I don't understand that the two halves need to be exactly the same.

standards.clusterText: Write and interpret numerical expressions.
standards.text: Use parentheses, brackets, or braces in numerical expressions, and evaluate expressions with these symbols.

wi.text: Use parentheses, brackets, or braces in numerical expressions, and evaluate expressions with these symbols.
wi.levelDescriptors:
CC Advanced: 
Accurately solve complex, multi-step real-world problems by applying their knowledge of grouping symbols and order of operations.

CC At Target: 
Accurately evaluate numerical expressions with parentheses, brackets, or braces, demonstrating understanding of the order of operations.

CC Approaching: 
Correctly evaluate numerical expressions containing parentheses alongside other operations (addition, subtraction, multiplication, division).

CC Emerging: 
Solve simple addition and subtraction problems where the parentheses are provided and dictate the only steps to take. (Ex: 5 + (3 - 1) )

standards.clusterText: Write and interpret numerical expressions.
standards.text: Write simple expressions that record calculations with numbers, and interpret numerical expressions without evaluating them. For example, express the calculation “add 8 and 7, then multiply by 2” as 2 × (8 + 7). Recognize that 3 × (18932 + 921) is three times as large as 18932 + 921, without having to calculate the indicated sum or product.

wi.text: Write simple expressions that record calculations with numbers and interpret numerical expressions without evaluating them. For example, express the calculation "add 8 and 7, then multiply by 2" as 2 x (8 + 7). Recognize that 3 x (18932 + 921) is three times as large as 18932 + 921, without having to calculate the indicated sum or product.
wi.levelDescriptors:
CC Advanced:
I can create complex expressions that involve multiple operations and apply them to real-world scenarios.
Example: I can write an expression to calculate the total cost of buying 3 pizzas at $12 each and 4 sodas at $2 each: (3 x $12) + (4 x $2) I can explain that this expression represents the cost of the pizzas plus the cost of the sodas.

CC At Target:
I can write simple expressions that record calculations with numbers and interpret numerical expressions without evaluating themfrom a given  real world scenario.
Example: "Add 8 and 7, then multiply by 2" is written as 2 x (8 + 7). I can recognize that 3 x (18932 + 921) is three times as large as 18932 + 921, without having to calculate the indicated sum or product.

CC Approaching:
I can write a simple expression with parentheses but may not understand the order of operations from a given scenerio.
Example: "Add 4 and 2, then multiply by 5" is written as (4 + 2) x 5, but I may not understand that the addition must be done first.

CC Emerging:
I can write a simple addition, subtraction, multiplication and/or division expression based on a given scenerio.
Example: "Add 5 and 3" is written as 5 + 3.

standards.clusterText: Analyze patterns and relationships.
standards.text: Generate two numerical patterns using two given rules. Identify apparent relationships between corresponding terms. Form ordered pairs consisting of corresponding terms from the two patterns, and graph the ordered pairs on a coordinate plane. For example, given the rule “Add 3” and the starting number 0, and given the rule “Add 6” and the starting number 0, generate terms in the resulting sequences, and observe that the terms in one sequence are twice the corresponding terms in the other sequence. Explain informally why this is so.

wi.text: Generate two numerical patterns using two given rules. Identify apparent relationships between corresponding terms. Form ordered pairs consisting of corresponding terms from the two patterns and graph the ordered pairs on a coordinate plane. For example, given the rule "Add 3" and the starting number 0, and given the rule "Add 6" and the starting number 0, generate terms in the resulting sequences, and observe that the terms in one sequence are twice the corresponding terms in the other sequence. Explain informally why this is so.
wi.levelDescriptors:
CC Advanced:
I can apply the concept of patterns and relationships to real-world scenarios and analyze data. For example, I can analyze the relationship between the number of hours worked and the amount of money earned, create a graph to represent this relationship, and use it to predict earnings for different work hours.

CC At Target:
 I can generate two numerical patterns with given rules, identify the relationship between corresponding terms, form ordered pairs, and graph them on a coordinate plane. For example, given the rule "Add 3" and the starting number 0, and given the rule "Add 6" and the starting number 0, I can generate the first five terms in each sequence (0, 3, 6, 9, 12 and 0, 6, 12, 18, 24), identify that the second sequence is always twice the first, form ordered pairs (0,0), (3,6), (6,12), (9,18), (12,24), and graph them on a coordinate plane.

CC Approaching:
I can generate two simple patterns with given rules and identify some corresponding terms. For example, I can find the first four terms in the pattern "Add 2" starting with 1 and the first four terms in the pattern "Add 4" starting with 1, and I can identify that the second pattern's numbers are always bigger than the first pattern's numbers.

CC Emerging:
I can identify the first few terms in a pattern given a simple rule. For example, I can find the first three numbers in a pattern that starts with 2 and adds 5 each time. Ex. Show me a pattern that increases by two and starts at 0 (i.e., 0, 2, 4, 6,. . . ).
Ex. Show me a pattern that increases by five and starts with 0 (i.e., 0, 5, 10, 15, . . . ).

standards.domainName: Number and Operations in Base Ten
standards.clusterText: Understand the place value system.
standards.text: Recognize that in a multi-digit number, a digit in one place represents 10 times as much as it represents in the place to its right and 1/10 of what it represents in the place to its left.

wi.text: Recognize that in a multi-digit number, a digit in one place represents 10 times as much as it represents in the place to its right and 1/10 of what it represents in the place to its left.
wi.levelDescriptors:
CC Advanced:
I can apply the relationship between place values to solve real-world problems involving money and measurement.
Ex: The student can explain that $4.50 is ten times greater than $0.45 and can use this understanding to solve problems like calculating the cost of ten items priced at $0.45 each. They can also apply this understanding to convert units of measurement, such as kilometers to meters or liters to milliliters.

CC At Target:
I can explain that the digit "4" in the number 400,000 represents 4 hundred thousands, which is ten times greater than the "4" in the number 40,000, which represents 4 ten thousands.
Ex: The student can explain that the "4" in 400,000 represents 4 hundred thousands, which is ten times greater than the "4" in the number 40,000, which represents 4 ten thousands. They can also explain that the "4" in 40,000 is ten times greater than the "4" in 4,000, which represents 4 thousands.

CC Approaching:
I can explain that the digit "4" in the number 4,567 represents 4 thousands, which is ten times greater than the "4" in the number 456, which represents 4 hundreds.
Ex: The student can explain that the "4" in 4,567 represents 4 thousands, which is ten times greater than the "4" in the number 456, which represents 4 hundreds. They can also explain that the "4" in 456 is ten times greater than the "4" in 45.6.

CC Emerging:
I can explain that a digit in the hundreds place is ten times greater than the same digit in the ten place.
Ex: The student can explain that the "2" in the number 225 represents 2 hundreds, which is ten times greater than the "2" in the number 25 which represents 2 tens.

standards.domainName: Number and Operations in Base Ten
standards.clusterText: Understand the place value system.
standards.text: Explain patterns in the number of zeros of the product when multiplying a number by powers of 10, and explain patterns in the placement of the decimal point when a decimal is multiplied or divided by a power of 10. Use whole-number exponents to denote powers of 10.

wi.text: Explain patterns in the number of zeros of the product when multiplying a number by powers of 10 and explain patterns in the placement of the decimal point when a decimal is multiplied or divided by a power of 10. Use whole-number exponents to denote powers of 10.
wi.levelDescriptors:
CC Advanced:
I can apply my understanding of multiplying and dividing decimals by powers of 10 to solve real-world problems, such as converting kilometers to meters or milligrams to grams. I can explain how the placement of the decimal point affects the units of measurement.

CC At Target:
I can explain that multiplying a number by 10^n (where n is a whole number) shifts the decimal point n places to the right, and dividing by 10^n shifts the decimal point n places to the left. I can use whole-number exponents to represent powers of 10. 

CC Approaching:
I can correctly multiply a whole number by 10, 100, and 1000 and explain that the number of zeros in the product matches the number of zeros in the power of 10.

CC Emerging:
I can identify that multiplying by 10 adds a zero to the end of a whole number because of the shift in the digits, but I struggle to explain why.

standards.domainName: Number and Operations in Base Ten
standards.clusterText: Understand the place value system.
standards.text: Read, write, and compare decimals to thousandths.

wi.text: Read, write, and compare decimals to thousandths. a. Read and write decimals to thousandths using base-ten numerals, number names, and expanded form, e.g., 347.392 = 3 x 100 + 4 x 10 + 7 x 1 + 3 x (1/10) + 9 x (1/100) + 2 x (1/1000). b. Compare decimals to thousandths based on meanings of the digits in each place and describe the result of the comparison using words and symbols ( >, =, and < ).
levelDescriptors:
CC Advanced:
I can apply my understanding of decimals to real-world scenarios. For example, I can compare the prices of three different items at the grocery store, using decimals to the thousandths place, and determine which item is the best value. I can also explain my reasoning using place value and symbols like >, =, and <.

CC At Target:
I can read, write, and compare decimals to thousandths using base-ten numerals, number names, and expanded form. For example, I can write 0.345 as three hundred forty-five thousandths and 3 x (1/10) + 4 x (1/100) + 5 x (1/1000). I can also compare decimals like 0.345 and 0.354, recognizing that 0.354 is greater because it has a larger digit in the hundredths place.

CC Approaching:
I can write a decimal number to the thousandths place using base-ten numerals, but I struggle with expanded form.

CC Emerging:
 I can identify the place value of the tenths digit in a decimal number.

CC Advanced:
I can accurately compare decimals to the thousandths place, explaining my reasoning based on place value and use symbols to show the relationship (e.g., "I compared 0.753 and 0.758 and explained that 0.753 < 0.758 because the thousandths place is smaller").
I can compare complex decimals, describing why one is greater or less than the other in multiple ways.

CC At Target:
I can compare decimals to the thousandths place by looking at each place value and use >, <, or = to show the comparison (e.g., "I know 0.456 > 0.452 because the hundredths are the same but 6 in the thousandths place is greater than 2").
I can explain my reasoning for comparing decimals based on the digits in each place.

CC Approaching:
I can compare simple decimals to the thousandths place with guidance, focusing on each place value (e.g., "With help, I compared 0.63 and 0.631 and saw that 0.63 < 0.631").
I can start to use >, <, and = symbols to compare decimals.

CC Emerging:
I can begin to understand that decimals are compared by looking at each place value, with help (e.g., "With support, I saw that 0.7 is greater than 0.68 by looking at the tenths place").
I can try using symbols like > and < to show which decimal is bigger or smaller, with guidance.

standards.domainName: Number and Operations in Base Ten
standards.clusterText: Understand the place value system.
standards.text: Read and write decimals to thousandths using base-ten numerals, number names, and expanded form, e.g., 347.392 = 3 × 100 + 4 × 10 + 7 × 1 + 3 × (1/10) + 9 × (1/100) + 2 × (1/1000).

standards.domainName: Number and Operations in Base Ten
standards.clusterText: Understand the place value system.
standards.text: Compare two decimals to thousandths based on meanings of the digits in each place, using >, =, and < symbols to record the results of comparisons.

standards.domainName: Number and Operations in Base Ten
standards.clusterText: Understand the place value system.
standards.text: Use place value understanding to round decimals to any place.

wi.text: Use place value understanding to generate estimates for problems in real-world situations, with decimals, using strategies such as mental math, benchmark numbers, compatible numbers, and rounding. Assess the reasonableness of their estimates (e.g., Is my estimate too low or too high? What degree of precision do I need for this situation?
wi.levelDescriptors:
CC Advanced:
I can use place value understanding to estimate the sum, difference, product, and quotient of decimals in complex real-world situations.
I can explain how my estimate helps me make informed decisions and solve problems efficiently.
I can communicate my reasoning clearly and effectively to others. 

CC At Target:
I can use mental math, benchmark numbers, compatible numbers, and rounding to estimate the sum, difference, and product of decimals in real-world situations.
I can explain my reasoning for choosing a particular strategy and how it helps me estimate.
I can assess the reasonableness of my estimate by considering the context of the problem and the level of precision needed.. 

CC Approaching:
I can estimate the sum of two decimals by rounding each number to the nearest tenth.
I can estimate the product of two decimals by rounding each number to the nearest whole number.
I can check the reasonableness of my estimate by comparing it to the actual answer. 

CC Emerging:
I can estimate the sum of two whole numbers by rounding each number to the nearest ten.
I can estimate the difference of two whole numbers by rounding each number to the nearest hundred.

standards.domainName: Number and Operations in Base Ten
standards.clusterText: Perform operations with multi-digit whole numbers and with decimals to hundredths.
standards.text: Fluently multiply multi-digit whole numbers using the standard algorithm.

wi.text: Flexibly and efficiently multiply multi-digit whole numbers using strategies or algorithms based on place value, area models, and the properties of operations.
wi.levelDescriptors:
CC Advanced:
I can multiply multi-digit numbers with decimals using the standard algorithm.
I can use my understanding of multiplication to solve real-world problems, such as calculating the area of a rectangular garden or the cost of buying multiple items at the store.
I can create my own strategies for multiplying multi-digit numbers, such as using mental math or a lattice method.

CC At Target:
I can multiply a two-digit number by a two-digit number using a standard algorithm based on place value and the distributive property.
I can explain the steps of the algorithm and how they relate to place value and the distributive property.
I can choose the most efficient strategy for multiplying two multi-digit numbers based on the numbers involved.

CC Approaching:
I can use a place value table to multiply a two-digit number by a one-digit number.
I can use the distributive property to break apart a multiplication problem into easier parts.
I can estimate the product of two multi-digit numbers.

CC Emerging:
I can skip-count by 10s and 100s to find the product of a multi-digit number and a one-digit number.
I can use repeated addition to find the product of a multi-digit number and a one-digit number.

standards.domainName: Number and Operations in Base Ten
standards.clusterText: Perform operations with multi-digit whole numbers and with decimals to hundredths.
standards.text: Find whole-number quotients of whole numbers with up to four-digit dividends and two-digit divisors, using strategies based on place value, the properties of operations, and/or the relationship between multiplication and division. Illustrate and explain the calculation by using equations, rectangular arrays, and/or area models.

wi.text: Find whole-number quotients of whole numbers with up to four-digit dividends and two-digit divisors, using strategies based on place value, the properties of operations, and/or the relationship between multiplication and division. Illustrate and explain the calculation by using equations, rectangular arrays, and/or area models.
wi.levelDescriptors:
CC Advanced:
 I can use mental math strategies to estimate the quotient of large numbers.
I can solve multi-step word problems involving division with large numbers.
I can explain how division is used in real-world situations, such as calculating the cost per unit or the number of equal groups that can be formed from a given quantity. 

CC At Target:
I can use long division to find the quotient of a four-digit number and a two-digit number.
I can explain my steps using equations, rectangular arrays, and area models.
I can recognize and apply the relationship between multiplication and division to check my answer. 

CC Approaching: 
I can use partial quotients to find the quotient of a three-digit number and a two-digit number.
I can explain my thinking using place value vocabulary. 

CC Emerging:
I can use repeated subtraction to find the quotient of a two-digit number and a single-digit number.
I can use repeated addition to find the produce of a two-digit number and a single-digit number.
I can use pictures or manipulatives to represent the division problem.
I can understand the inverse operation of multiplication and division of fact famlies.

standards.domainName: Number and Operations in Base Ten
standards.clusterText: Perform operations with multi-digit whole numbers and with decimals to hundredths.
standards.text: Add, subtract, multiply, and divide decimals to hundredths, using concrete models or drawings and strategies based on place value, properties of operations, and/or the relationship between addition and subtraction; relate the strategy to a written method and explain the reasoning used.

wi.text: Add, subtract, multiply, and divide decimals to hundredths, using concrete models or drawings and strategies based on place value, properties of operations, and/or the relationship between addition and subtraction; relate the strategy to a written method and explain the reasoning used.
wi.levelDescriptors:
CC Advanced:
I can apply my understanding of decimals to solve real-world problems involving area, perimeter, volume, and other complex calculations.
I can create my own strategies for adding, subtracting, multiplying, and dividing decimals based on my understanding of place value and properties of operations.
I can explain my reasoning clearly and concisely, using mathematical vocabulary and notation.
I can use technology, such as spreadsheets or calculators, to solve complex problems involving decimals.. 

CC At Target:
I can add, subtract, multiply, and divide decimals to hundredths using concrete models or drawings.
I can explain my reasoning for choosing a specific strategy based on place value, properties of operations, and the relationship between addition and subtraction.
I can solve multi-step word problems involving addition, subtraction, multiplication, and division of decimals with accuracy.
I can relate the strategies I use with concrete models to written methods for solving problems. 

CC Approaching:
I can add and subtract decimals to the tenths place using a place value chart and manipulatives.
I can explain the relationship between addition and subtraction of decimals using concrete examples.
I can solve simple word problems involving addition and subtraction of decimals with some assistance. 

CC Emerging:
I can add and subtract whole numbers using manipulatives, but I struggle to apply this understanding to decimals.
I can estimate the sum or difference of decimals, but I have difficulty using place value to solve problems accurately.

standards.clusterText: Use equivalent fractions as a strategy to add and subtract fractions.
standards.text: Add and subtract fractions with unlike denominators (including mixed numbers) by replacing given fractions with equivalent fractions in such a way as to produce an equivalent sum or difference of fractions with like denominators. For example, 2/3 + 5/4 = 8/12 + 15/12 = 23/12. (In general, a/b + c/d = (ad + bc)/bd.)

wi.text: Add and subtract fractions and mixed numbers using flexible and efficient strategies, including renaming fractions with equivalent fractions. Justify using visual models (e.g., tape diagrams or number lines) and equations. For example, 2/3 + 5/4 = 8/12 + 15/12 = 23/12.
wi.levelDescriptors:
CC Advanced: 
I can add and subtract fractions and mixed numbers efficiently using mental math strategies.
I can apply my understanding of adding and subtracting fractions to solve real-world problems, such as calculating the total amount of fabric needed for a project or figuring out how much time it takes to complete two tasks.
I can explain my solutions using sophisticated vocabulary and complex sentences.
I can also explain the reasoning behind my chosen strategies and connect them to other mathematical concepts. 

CC At Target:
I can add and subtract fractions and mixed numbers with different denominators by finding a common denominator and using equivalent fractions.
I can justify my solutions using visual models (e.g., tape diagrams or number lines) and equations.
I can explain my reasoning clearly and concisely. 

CC Approaching:
I can add and subtract fractions with the same denominator by finding a common denominator.
I can add and subtract fractions with different denominators using visual models like number lines, but I sometimes make mistakes when converting fractions to equivalent fractions.
I can explain my reasoning using simple sentences. 

CC Emerging:
I can add and subtract fractions with the same denominator by counting the total number of parts in the numerator.
I can add and subtract fractions with different denominators by drawing pictures, but I struggle to explain my reasoning.

standards.clusterText: Use equivalent fractions as a strategy to add and subtract fractions.
standards.text: Solve word problems involving addition and subtraction of fractions referring to the same whole, including cases of unlike denominators, e.g., by using visual fraction models or equations to represent the problem. Use benchmark fractions and number sense of fractions to estimate mentally and assess the reasonableness of answers. For example, recognize an incorrect result 2/5 + 1/2 = 3/7, by observing that 3/7 < 1/2.

wi.text: Solve word problems involving addition and subtraction of fractions referring to the same whole using visual fraction models or equations to represent the problem. Use benchmark fractions and number sense of fractions to estimate mentally and assess the reasonableness of answers. For example, recognize an incorrect result 2/5 + 1/2 = 3/7, by observing that 3/7 <1/2.
wi.levelDescriptors:
CC Advanced:
I can apply my understanding of adding and subtracting fractions and mixed numbers to solve real-world problems.
For example, I can calculate the total amount of fabric needed to make two curtains, each requiring 2 1/2 yards of fabric.
I can also explain my reasoning and justify my solutions using clear and concise language. 

CC At Target:
I can add and subtract fractions with the same denominator by writing equivalent fractions with a common denominator.
I can add and subtract fractions with different denominators by finding a common denominator using prime factorization. 

CC Approaching:
I can add and subtract fractions with different denominators by finding a common denominator using prime factorization or using multiples without visual models

CC Emerging:
I can add and subtract fractions with the same denominator by counting the parts of a visual model
I can add and subtract fractions with different denominators by finding a common denominator using multiples with visual models

standards.clusterText: Apply and extend previous understandings of multiplication and division to multiply and divide fractions.
standards.text: Interpret a fraction as division of the numerator by the denominator (a/b = a÷b). Solve word problems involving division of whole numbers leading to answers in the form of fractions or mixed numbers, e.g., by using visual fraction models or equations to represent the problem. For example, interpret 3/4 as the result of dividing 3 by 4, noting that 3/4 multiplied by 4 equals 3, and that when 3 wholes are shared equally among 4 people each person has a share of size 3/4. If 9 people want to share a 50-pound sack of rice equally by weight, how many pounds of rice should each person get? Between what two whole numbers does your answer lie?

wi.text: Interpret a fraction as an equal sharing division situation, where a quantity (the numerator) is divided into equal parts (the denominator). Solve word problems involving division of whole numbers leading to answers in the form of fractions or mixed numbers, by using visual fraction models (e.g., tape diagrams or area models) or equations to represent the problem. For example, when 3 wholes are shared equally among 4 people each person has a share of size 3/4. If 9 people want to share a 50-pound sack of rice equally by weight, how many pounds of rice should each person get? Between what two whole numbers does your answer lie?
wi.levelDescriptors:
CC Advanced:
I can apply my understanding of fractions and division to solve real-world problems involving equal sharing and interpret the results in context.
Ex: I can calculate the amount of fabric needed to make 3 identical scarves if each scarf requires 2/3 yards of fabric. I can then determine the cost of the fabric based on its price per yard and apply my knowledge of fractions to calculate the total cost. 

CC At Target:
I can interpret a fraction as an equal sharing division situation and solve word problems involving division of whole numbers leading to answers in the form of fractions or mixed numbers, using visual fraction models or equations.
Ex: If 9 people want to share a 50-pound sack of rice equally by weight, each person should get 50/9 pounds of rice. This is a little more than 5 pounds (5 and 5/9 pounds) because 50 divided by 9 is 5 with a remainder of 5.

CC Approaching:
I can divide a whole number into equal parts and represent the answer as a fraction, but I struggle to solve word problems involving division of whole numbers leading to answers in the form of fractions or mixed numbers.
Ex: I can divide 5 pizzas into 8 equal slices and represent each slice as 5/8. However, I struggle to solve a word problem like "If 7 friends want to share 3 pizzas equally, how much pizza does each friend get?"

CC Emerging:
I can divide a whole number into equal parts but struggle to represent the answer as a fraction.
Ex: Given 4 cookies to share equally among 3 friends, I can divide the cookies into 3 groups but cannot represent each friend's share as 4/3

standards.clusterText: Apply and extend previous understandings of multiplication and division to multiply and divide fractions.
standards.text: Apply and extend previous understandings of multiplication to multiply a fraction or whole number by a fraction.

wi.text: Apply and extend previous understandings of multiplication to multiply a fraction times a whole number (e.g., 2/3 x 4) or a fraction times a fraction (e.g., 2/3 x 4/5), including mixed numbers. Represent word problems involving multiplication of fractions using visual models to develop flexible and efficient strategies. For example, use a visual fraction model to show (2/3) × 4 = 8/3, and create a story context for this equation. Do the same with (2/3) × (4/5) = 8/15. Find the area of a rectangle with fractional side lengths by tiling it with unit squares of the appropriate unit fraction side lengths and show that the area is the same as would be found by multiplying the side lengths. Multiply fractional side lengths to find areas of rectangles and represent fraction products as rectangular areas.
levelDescriptors:
CC Advanced:
I can find the area of a rectangle with fractional side lengths by tiling it with unit squares of the appropriate unit fraction side lengths and show that the area is the same as would be found by multiplying the side lengths. I can also apply this understanding to real-world situations, such as calculating the area of a garden plot with fractional dimensions or determining the amount of fabric needed for a project with fractional measurements.

CC At Target:
I can represent word problems involving multiplication of fractions using visual models to develop flexible and efficient strategies. For example, I can use a visual fraction model to show (2/3) × 4 = 8/3 and create a story context for this equation. I can also do the same with (2/3) × (4/5) = 8/15. 

CC Approaching:
I can multiply a whole number by a fraction with a visual model, but I struggle to create a story context for the equation.

CC Emerging:
I can use visual models (like fraction circles or drawings) to show what a fraction represents (e.g., showing 2/3 of a circle) and can identify the whole and the parts.

CC Advanced:
I can calculate the area of a rectangle with fractional side lengths by tiling with unit squares and explain why tiling gives the same result as multiplying the side lengths (e.g., "I tiled a rectangle with sides 1/2 and 2/3 using unit squares and showed the area equals 1/2 x 2/3").
I can represent products of fractions as areas and apply this understanding to solve real-world problems with rectangles of fractional side lengths.

CC At Target:
I can find the area of a rectangle with fractional side lengths by tiling with unit squares and by multiplying the fractions (e.g., "I found the area of a rectangle with sides 3/4 and 2/5 by tiling it and confirmed it by multiplying 3/4 x 2/5").
I can explain how the product of two fractions represents the area of a rectangle with fractional side lengths.

CC Approaching:
I can find the area of a simple rectangle with fractional side lengths by tiling with unit fractions, with some guidance (e.g., "With help, I used unit squares to find the area of a rectangle with side lengths 1/2 and 1/3").
I can start to understand that multiplying fractional side lengths gives the area of a rectangle, with support.

CC Emerging:
I can begin to see that tiling a rectangle with fractional unit squares shows its area, with guidance (e.g., "With help, I used unit squares with side lengths 1/2 to cover a rectangle and find its area").
I can try using fractional units to cover a rectangle and start to understand how this relates to finding the area, with support.

standards.clusterText: Apply and extend previous understandings of multiplication and division to multiply and divide fractions.
standards.text: Interpret the product (a/b) ×q as a parts of a partition of q into b equal parts; equivalently, as the result of a sequence of operations a×q÷b. For example, use a visual fraction model to show (2/3) × 4 = 8/3, and create a story context for this equation. Do the same with (2/3) × (4/5) = 8/15. (In general, (a/b) × (c/d) = ac/bd.)

standards.clusterText: Apply and extend previous understandings of multiplication and division to multiply and divide fractions.
standards.text: Find the area of a rectangle with fractional side lengths by tiling it with unit squares of the appropriate unit fraction side lengths, and show that the area is the same as would be found by multiplying the side lengths. Multiply fractional side lengths to find areas of rectangles, and represent fraction products as rectangular areas.

standards.clusterText: Apply and extend previous understandings of multiplication and division to multiply and divide fractions.
standards.text: Interpret multiplication as scaling (resizing), by:

wi.text: Interpret multiplication as scaling (resizing) by estimating whether a product will be larger or smaller than a given factor on the basis of the size of the other factor, without performing the indicated multiplication. Explain why multiplying a given number by a fraction greater than 1 results in a product greater than the given number and explain why multiplying a given number by a fraction less than 1 results in a product smaller than the given number. Relate the principle of fraction equivalence to the effect of multiplying or dividing a fraction by 1 or an equivalent form of 1 (e.g., 3/3, 5/5).
levelDescriptors:
CC Advanced:
I can apply the concept of scaling to real-world situations and explain the effect of multiplying by fractions greater than or less than 1.

CC At Target:
I can estimate whether a product will be larger or smaller than a given factor based on the size of the other factor, without performing the multiplication.

CC Approaching:
I can sometimes explain why multiplying by a fraction greater than 1 makes the product larger. 

CC Emerging:
I can use pictures or objects to show that multiplying a whole number or fraction by a whole number makes something bigger or smaller.

CC Advanced:
I can explain why multiplying or dividing a fraction by an equivalent form of 1 (e.g., 4/4 or 6/6) does not change its value and use this principle to create equivalent fractions (e.g., "I multiplied 1/2 by 3/3 to make 3/6, which is the same value as 1/2").
I can apply the concept of fraction equivalence to simplify or scale fractions in real-world situations, explaining why the fraction remains unchanged.

CC At Target:
I can show that multiplying or dividing a fraction by an equivalent form of 1 (like 5/5 or 2/2) keeps the fraction equal in value (e.g., "I multiplied 2/3 by 2/2 to get 4/6, which is still equal to 2/3").
I can use this principle to create equivalent fractions by multiplying or dividing by forms of 1.

CC Approaching:
I can create simple equivalent fractions by multiplying by forms of 1, with some guidance (e.g., "With help, I multiplied 3/4 by 2/2 to make 6/8 and learned it is equal to 3/4").
I can start to understand that multiplying a fraction by an equivalent of 1 does not change its value, with support.

CC Emerging:
I can begin to understand that multiplying a fraction by a form of 1, like 3/3, keeps it the same, with guidance (e.g., "With help, I saw that 1/2 stays the same when I multiply by 2/2").
I can try to use simple examples to see that multiplying by forms of 1 keeps fractions equal, with support.

standards.text: Comparing the size of a product to the size of one factor on the basis of the size of the other factor, without performing the indicated multiplication.

standards.clusterText: Apply and extend previous understandings of multiplication and division to multiply and divide fractions.
standards.text: Explaining why multiplying a given number by a fraction greater than 1 results in a product greater than the given number (recognizing multiplication by whole numbers greater than 1 as a familiar case); explaining why multiplying a given number by a fraction less than 1 results in a product smaller than the given number; and relating the principle of fraction equivalence a/b = (n×a)/(n×b) to the effect of multiplying a/b by 1.

standards.clusterText: Apply and extend previous understandings of multiplication and division to multiply and divide fractions.
standards.text: Solve real world problems involving multiplication of fractions and mixed numbers, e.g., by using visual fraction models or equations to represent the problem.

wi.text: Solve real-world problems involving multiplication of fractions and mixed numbers by using visual fraction models (e.g., tape diagrams, area models, or number lines) and equations to represent the problem. Use benchmark fractions and number sense of fractions to estimate mentally and assess the reasonableness of answers.
wi.levelDescriptors:
CC Advanced:
I can create and solve my own real-world problems that involve multiplying fractions and mixed numbers, justifying my solution with both a visual model and an equation.

CC At Target:
I can solve given real-world problems that involve multiplying fractions using visual models like tape diagrams and area models, and I can represent the problem with an equation.

CC Approaching Students:
I can use a number line to solve real-world problems involving multiplication of a whole number by a unit fraction.

CC Emerging Students:
I can use visual models like fraction circles to represent multiplication of a whole number by a unit fraction.

standards.clusterText: Apply and extend previous understandings of multiplication and division to multiply and divide fractions.
standards.text: Apply and extend previous understandings of division to divide unit fractions by whole numbers and whole numbers by unit fractions.

wi.text: Apply and extend previous understandings of division to divide unit fractions by whole numbers (e.g., 1/3 ÷ 4) and whole numbers by unit fractions (e.g., 4 ÷ 1/5). Students able to multiply fractions can develop strategies to divide fractions by reasoning about the relationship between multiplication and division. But division of a fraction by a fraction is not a requirement at this grade. Interpret and represent division of a unit fraction by a non-zero whole number as an equal sharing division situation. For example, create a story context for (1/3) ÷ 4, and use a visual fraction model to show the quotient. Use the relationship between multiplication and division to explain that (1/3) ÷ 4 = 1/12 because (1/12) × 4 = 1/3. Interpret and represent division of a whole number by a unit fraction as a measurement division situation. For example, create a story context for 4 ÷ (1/5), and use a visual fraction model to show the quotient. Use the relationship between multiplication and division to explain that 4 ÷ (1/5) = 20 because 20 × (1/5) = 4.
levelDescriptors:
CC Advanced
I can create a real-world problem that involves dividing a unit fraction by a whole number or a whole number by a unit fraction. I can solve my problem, justify my solution using a visual model and an equation, and explain why my answer makes sense. Ex. Maria has 3 pizzas, and she wants to divide each pizza equally among her friends, giving each friend ⅙ of a whole pizza. How many friends can she share with?

CC At Target
I can solve real-world problems involving multiplication of fractions and mixed numbers by using visual fraction models and equations. For example, I can use a tape diagram to represent the problem "If a recipe calls for 1 1/2 cups of flour, and I want to make 2/3 of the recipe, how much flour do I need?" and write the equation 1 1/2 x 2/3 = 1.

CC Approaching
I can use a visual fraction model to solve a simple multiplication problem with fractions, but I may struggle to write the corresponding equation. For example, I can use a number line to find the product of 1/4 x 3, but I may not be able to write the equation 1/4 x 3 = 3/4.

CC Emerging
I can identify the correct visual model to represent a simple multiplication problem with fractions. For example, I can choose a tape diagram to represent 1/2 x 2.

CC Advanced:
I can apply my understanding of division of a whole number by a unit fraction to solve real-world problems. For example, I can use division to find out how many 1/5-cup servings of juice I can get from 4 cups of juice. I can explain my reasoning clearly and concisely using mathematical vocabulary. For example, I can explain that 4 ÷ (1/5) = 20 because dividing 4 by 1/5 is the same as multiplying 4 by the reciprocal of 1/5, which is 5.

CC At Target:
I can interpret and represent division of a whole number by a unit fraction as a measurement division situation. For example, I can understand that 4 ÷ (1/5) represents dividing 4 objects into groups of 1/5 each, and that this is the same as finding out how many groups of 1/5 are in 4. I can use a visual fraction model to represent the division of a whole number by a unit fraction. For example, I can use a rectangular fraction model to show that 4 ÷ (1/5) is the same as dividing a rectangle with an area of 4 square units into 5 equal rows, and that the quotient is the number of rows. I can use the relationship between multiplication and division to explain that 4 ÷ (1/5) = 20 because 20 × (1/5) = 4.

CC Approaching:
I can use a visual model to show the division of a whole number by a unit fraction, recognizing that it represents partitioning the whole into groups of that unit fraction size.
Example: Given 4 ÷ (1/5), I can draw a rectangle representing "4" and divide it into five equal parts to represent finding how many "fifths" are in the whole.

CC Emerging:
I can demonstrate the meaning of dividing a whole number by a unit fraction using concrete objects or drawings, focusing on the idea of equal sharing. Ex: Given the problem 2 ÷ ½, the student can: Take two whole objects (e.g., cookies) and divide each cookie into halves. Count the total number of halves (4) to show the result of the division.

CC Advanced:
I can apply my understanding of dividing unit fractions and whole numbers to solve complex real-world problems. I can create my own word problems involving the division of unit fractions and whole numbers. I can explain the concept of dividing unit fractions and whole numbers to others. I can use my knowledge of dividing unit fractions and whole numbers in other areas of mathematics, such as algebra or geometry. I can solve problems like: Ex. A recipe calls for 2/3 cup of chopped nuts. If I only have 1/4 cup of chopped nuts, how many batches of the recipe can I make? Ex. A train travels 3/4 of a mile in 1/5 of an hour. What is the train's speed in miles per hour?

CC At Target:
I can use visual fraction models and equations to represent and solve real-world problems involving the division of unit fractions by non-zero whole numbers and the division of whole numbers by unit fractions. I can explain my reasoning using mathematical language. I can solve problems like: Ex. How much chocolate will each person get if 4 people share 1/3 lb. of chocolate equally? (Each person gets 1/12 lb. of chocolate.) Ex. How many 1/5-cup servings are in 4 cups of raisins? (There are 20 servings of size 1/5-cup of raisins.)

CC Approaching:
I can divide a unit fraction, like 1/2, into equal parts using a visual model. I can write a simple equation to represent the division of a unit fraction by a whole number, like 1/2 ÷ 3. I can solve simple real-world problems involving the division of a unit fraction by a whole number, like sharing 1/2 cup of flour equally among 3 friends.

CC Emerging:
I can split a whole object, like a pizza, into equal parts. I can identify unit fractions, like halves, thirds, fourths, eighths.

standards.clusterText: Convert like measurement units within a given measurement system.
standards.text: Convert among different-sized standard measurement units within a given measurement system (e.g., convert 5 cm to 0.05 m), and use these conversions in solving multi-step, real world problems.

wi.text: Convert among different-sized standard measurement units within a given measurement system (e.g., convert 5 cm to 0.05 m), and use these conversions in solving multi-step, real-world problems.
wi.levelDescriptors:
CC Advanced:
Apply unit conversions to solve complex, real-world problems that involve multiple steps and multiple units. Explain the reasoning behind my conversions and calculations. Choose the most appropriate units for a given situation.

CC At Target:
Convert fluently between different-sized standard units within the same measurement system (e.g., convert 5 cm to 0.05 m).
Use these conversions to solve multi-step, real-world problems.

CC Approaching:
Use a ruler to measure length in inches and centimeters. Recognize that there are different units within the same measurement system (e.g., inches and feet are both units of length). Begin to make simple conversions between units within the same system (e.g., 12 inches = 1 foot). Ex: A student measures the length of a pencil in inches and then converts it to centimeters using a conversion chart. They can explain that there are 2.54 centimeters in 1 inch.

CC Emerging:
Count objects to measure length. Ex. Identify different units of measurement (e.g., inches, feet) but have difficulty relating them to each other.

standards.clusterText: Represent and interpret data.
standards.text: Make a line plot to display a data set of measurements in fractions of a unit (1/2, 1/4, 1/8). Use operations on fractions for this grade to solve problems involving information presented in line plots. For example, given different measurements of liquid in identical beakers, find the amount of liquid each beaker would contain if the total amount in all the beakers were redistributed equally.

wi.text: Make a line plot to display a data set of measurements in fractions of a unit (1/2, 1/4, 1/8). Use operations on fractions for this grade to solve problems involving information presented in line plots. For example, given different measurements of liquid in identical beakers, find the amount of liquid each beaker would contain if the total amount in all the beakers were redistributed equally.
wi.levelDescriptors:
CC Advanced:
I can create line plots that show data using fractions for more than one category. I can use my knowledge of fractions to solve real-world problems based on the information in the line plot and explain my thinking clearly. Ex: Students measure the length of different colored ribbons used in a craft project (red, blue, green) to the nearest ¼ inch. They create a line plot with color-coded Xs to display the length of each ribbon piece. They then answer questions like, "How much longer is the longest blue ribbon than the shortest red ribbon?" or "What is the total length of all the green ribbons used?"

CC At Target:
I can create a line plot to show measurements in fractions (like ½, ¼, ⅛). I can use addition, subtraction, and other fraction operations to answer questions about the data shown on the line plot and explain my thinking. Ex: Students measure the rainfall each day for a week to the nearest ¼ inch and record their data. They create a line plot to display the rainfall data. They then answer questions like, "How much more rain fell on Tuesday than on Thursday?" or "What was the total rainfall for the week?"

CC Approaching:
I can organize data in a tally chart and measure lengths to the nearest ¼ inch using a ruler. I can make a good guess about the value of a fraction on a number line.
Ex: Students are given a collection of leaves and asked to measure the width of each leaf to the nearest ¼ inch. They record their measurements in a tally chart. They then practice placing fractions like ¾, ¼, and 1 ½ on a number line.

CC Emerging:
I can draw a simple picture to represent data, count how many times something happens in the data, and name the different values in the data.
Example: Students collect data on their classmates' favorite fruits (apple, banana, orange). They draw a picture to represent each fruit choice (e.g., a circle for each apple). They then count how many of each fruit picture they drew and name the different fruits in their data.

standards.clusterText: Geometric measurement: understand concepts of volume and relate volume to multiplication and to addition.
standards.text: Recognize volume as an attribute of solid figures and understand concepts of volume measurement.

wi.text: Recognize volume as an attribute of solid figures and understand concepts of volume measurement. a. A cube with side length 1 unit, called a "unit cube", is said to have "one cubic unit" of volume, and can be used to measure volume. b. A solid figure which can be packed without gaps or overlaps using n unit cubes is said to have a volume of n cubic units.
levelDescriptors:
CC Advanced:
I can calculate the volume of irregular solid figures by decomposing them into smaller shapes. I can apply my understanding of volume to solve real-world problems, such as determining the amount of water needed to fill a pool. I can explain the relationship between volume and density.

CC At Target:
I can calculate the volume of a rectangular prism by multiplying its length, width, and height. I can explain that the volume of a solid figure is measured in cubic units.

CC Approaching: I can measure the volume of a rectangular prism by counting the number of unit cubes it can hold. I can explain that the volume of a solid figure is the amount of space it occupies.  I can recognize that a solid figure with a larger volume can hold more objects than a solid figure with a smaller volume.

CC Emerging:
I can identify the volume of a cube with side length 1 unit as "one cubic unit." I can recognize that some solid figures can be filled with unit cubes.

CC Advanced:
I can explain why packing a solid figure completely with unit cubes gives its volume and use this principle to find and justify the volume of different shapes (e.g., "I packed a box with 24 unit cubes and explained that the volume is 24 cubic units because it’s fully filled").
I can use unit cubes to compare volumes of different shapes and explain how the number of cubes relates to the volume of each shape.

CC At Target:
I can find the volume of a solid figure by counting the number of unit cubes that fit inside without gaps or overlaps (e.g., "I used 12 unit cubes to fill a rectangular prism, so the volume is 12 cubic units").
I can explain that the volume of a shape is the total number of unit cubes that fill it.

CC Approaching:
I can determine the volume of a simple shape by counting the unit cubes that fill it, with some guidance (e.g., "With help, I counted 8 cubes in a small box to find that its volume is 8 cubic units").
I can start to understand that filling a shape with unit cubes gives the shape’s volume, with support.

CC Emerging:
I can begin to understand that filling a solid figure with unit cubes helps measure its volume, with guidance (e.g., "With support, I used cubes to see how many fit in a small box").
I can try counting unit cubes to find the volume of simple shapes, with help.

standards.text: Measure volumes by counting unit cubes, using cubic cm, cubic in, cubic ft, and improvised units.

wi.text: Measure volumes by counting unit cubes, using cubic cm, cubic in., cubic ft., and improvised units.
wi.levelDescriptors:
CC Advanced:
I can find the volume of a cylinder by using the formula: Volume = πr²h, where r is the radius and h is the height. I can use my knowledge of volume to solve real-world problems, such as calculating the amount of water needed to fill a pool or the amount of soil needed to fill a garden bed. I can explain the relationship between the volume of an object and its dimensions.

CC At Target:
I can find the volume of a rectangular prism by using the formula: Volume = Length x Width x Height. I can use cubic centimeters, cubic inches, and cubic feet to measure the volume of different objects. I can use improvised units to measure the volume of irregular objects.

CC Approaching:
I can find the volume of a rectangular prism by counting the unit cubes needed to fill it. I can use cubic centimeters to measure the volume of a rectangular prism.

CC Emerging:
I can determine the volume of a rectangular prism by counting unit cubes along all three edges. I can explain that the volume of a rectangular prism is the length x width x height. I can solve word problems involving the volume of rectangular prisms.

standards.clusterText: Geometric measurement: understand concepts of volume and relate volume to multiplication and to addition.
standards.text: Relate volume to the operations of multiplication and addition and solve real world and mathematical problems involving volume.

wi.text: Relate volume to the operations of multiplication and addition and solve real- world and mathematical problems involving volume. a. Find the volume of a right rectangular prism with whole-number side lengths by packing it with unit cubes and show that the volume is the same as would be found by multiplying the edge lengths, equivalently by multiplying the height by the area of the base. Represent threefold whole-number products as volumes, e.g., to represent the associative property of multiplication. b. Apply the formulas V = l x w x h and V = B x h for rectangular prisms to find volumes of right rectangular prisms with whole number edge lengths in the context of solving real- world and mathematical problems. c. Recognize volume as additive. Find volumes of solid figures composed of two non-overlapping right rectangular prisms by adding the volumes of the non-overlapping parts, applying this technique to solve real- world problems.
levelDescriptors:
CC Advanced Students will: 
 I can explain the relationship between volume and the operations of multiplication and addition.
I can use the concept of volume to solve complex real-world problems, such as calculating the amount of concrete needed to build a patio or the amount of water needed to fill a swimming pool.
I can extend the concept of volume to other three-dimensional shapes, such as cylinders and cones.
I can create my own formulas for finding the volume of different shapes.

CC At Target Students will:
I can find the volume of a rectangular prism by packing it with unit cubes and multiplying the edge lengths.
I can use the formula V = l x w x h to find the volume of a rectangular prism with whole-number side lengths.
I can apply the formulas V = l x w x h and V = B x h to find the volumes of right rectangular prisms with whole-number edge lengths in real-world and mathematical problems.
I can recognize volume as additive and find the volumes of solid figures composed of two non-overlapping right rectangular prisms by adding the volumes of the non-overlapping parts.
I can solve real-world problems involving the volume of rectangular prisms.

CC Approaching Students will:
I can find the volume of a rectangular prism by counting unit cubes and multiplying the length, width, and height.
I can explain that the volume of a rectangular prism is the same as the area of the base multiplied by the height.
I can use the formula V = l x w x h to find the volume of a rectangular prism with whole-number side lengths.

CC Emerging Students will:
I can find the volume of a rectangular prism by counting the number of unit cubes that fit inside it.
I can explain that the volume of a rectangular prism is the length x width x height.
I can use the formula V = l x w x h to find the volume of a rectangular prism.

CC Advanced:
I can find the volume of rectangular prisms in complex real-world situations using the formulas 
𝑉 = 𝑙 × 𝑤 × ℎ and 𝑉 = 𝐵 × ℎ V=B×h, and explain why both formulas give the same result (e.g., "I used both formulas to find the volume of a shipping box and confirmed they match").
I can solve multi-step volume problems involving rectangular prisms by applying the correct formula and justifying each step.

CC At Target:
I can use the formulas 
𝑉 = 𝑙 × 𝑤 × ℎ  and 𝑉 = 𝐵 × ℎ to find the volume of a rectangular prism with whole-number edge lengths (e.g., "I calculated the volume of a box with length 4, width 3, and height 2 as 4 x 3 x 2 = 24 cubic units").
I can choose the appropriate formula and apply it correctly in mathematical and real-world volume problems.

CC Approaching:
I can find the volume of a rectangular prism by filling in values for length, width, and height in the formula 𝑉 = 𝑙 × 𝑤 × ℎ , with some guidance (e.g., "With help, I used the formula to find the volume of a prism with length 5, width 2, and height 3").
I can start to understand how the volume formula calculates the space inside a rectangular prism, with support.

CC Emerging:
I can begin to use the formula 𝑉 = 𝑙 × 𝑤 × ℎ to find the volume of simple prisms, with guidance (e.g., "With support, I used 3 x 2 x 1 to calculate the volume of a small box").
I can try substituting values in the volume formula to find the space inside a rectangular shape, with help.

CC Advanced:
I can find the total volume of complex shapes by breaking them into two or more non-overlapping rectangular prisms, calculating each part, and adding the results (e.g., "I split a storage unit into two sections and found the total volume by adding each section's volume").
I can apply the additive volume property to solve real-world problems, explaining why adding the separate volumes gives the total.

CC At Target:
I can find the volume of a figure made of two non-overlapping rectangular prisms by calculating each prism’s volume and adding them together (e.g., "I found the volume of a combined shape by adding the volumes of the two parts").
I can explain that adding the volumes of non-overlapping parts gives the total volume of the shape.

CC Approaching:
I can start finding the volume of a figure made of two prisms by calculating each prism’s volume with help and adding them (e.g., "With guidance, I calculated the volume of each section and added them").
I can understand that combining volumes of separate parts gives a total volume, with support.

CC Emerging:
I can begin to understand that the volume of a figure with two parts can be found by adding each part's volume, with help (e.g., "With support, I found the volume of each part and added them to get the total").
I can try using simple volumes to see how separate parts add up to make a whole, with guidance.

standards.clusterText: Graph points on the coordinate plane to solve real-world and mathematical problems.
standards.text: Use a pair of perpendicular number lines, called axes, to define a coordinate system, with the intersection of the lines (the origin) arranged to coincide with the 0 on each line and a given point in the plane located by using an ordered pair of numbers, called its coordinates. Understand that the first number indicates how far to travel from the origin in the direction of one axis, and the second number indicates how far to travel in the direction of the second axis, with the convention that the names of the two axes and the coordinates correspond (e.g., x-axis and x-coordinate, y-axis and y-coordinate).

wi.text: Use a pair of perpendicular number lines, called axes, to define a coordinate system, with the intersection of the lines (the origin) arranged to coincide with the 0 on each line and a given point in the plane located by using an ordered pair of numbers, called its coordinates. Understand that the first number indicates how far to travel from the origin in the direction of one axis, and the second number indicates how far to travel in the direction of the second axis, with the convention that the names of the two axes and the coordinates correspond (e.g., x-axis and x- coordinate, y-axis and y-coordinate).
wi.levelDescriptors:
CC Advanced:
I can use the coordinate plane to represent and solve problems. This includes finding distances between points, plotting shapes, and applying the coordinate plane to real-world situations like reading maps or designing layouts. Example: A student is given a map on a coordinate plane with points representing landmarks. They can calculate the distance between two landmarks, plot a route between multiple points, or even design their own map with specific locations.

CC At Target:
I can create a coordinate plane with labeled axes and accurately plot points using ordered pairs (x, y). I understand that the first number tells me how far to move along the x-axis, and the second number tells me how far to move along the y-axis. Example: A student can draw a coordinate plane with the x-axis and y-axis labeled, including numbers. If given the ordered pair (3, 5), they can correctly move 3 units to the right from the origin and then 5 units up to plot the point.

CC Approaching:
Draw two perpendicular lines. Label the lines with numbers, starting from zero on both lines. Place a dot on the lines to represent a point. Use one number to describe the location of the point on one of the lines.

CC Emerging:
I can draw two lines and mark points on them. I am starting to understand that lines and points can be used to show locations. Example: A student can draw two lines on a paper, though they might not be perfectly perpendicular. They can label the lines with some numbers, but they may not start from zero or be in order. standards.clusterText: Classify two-dimensional figures into categories based on their properties.
standards.text: Understand that attributes belonging to a category of two-dimensional figures also belong to all subcategories of that category. For example, all rectangles have four right angles and squares are rectangles, so all squares have four right angles.

wi.levelDescriptors:
CC Advanced:
I can use my knowledge about shape categories and their attributes to solve real-world problems and explain my reasoning.
Example: A student is challenged to design a tabletop using only quadrilaterals. They can use their knowledge of different quadrilateral types (squares, rectangles, parallelograms, trapezoids) and their properties to create a functional and aesthetically pleasing design, explaining their choices based on shape attributes.

CC At Target:
I can explain why shapes within the same category share the same attributes, even if they look different.
Example: A student can use a Venn diagram to show the relationship between rectangles and squares. They can explain that all squares belong inside the rectangle circle because they share all rectangle attributes (4 sides, 4 right angles, opposite sides equal), but not all rectangles are squares.

CC Approaching:
I can identify and compare the attributes (sides, angles, etc.) of different two-dimensional shapes, including shapes that belong to the same category.
Example: Given a set of quadrilaterals, including squares, rectangles, and trapezoids, a student can sort them by the number of parallel sides. They can identify that some quadrilaterals have two pairs of parallel sides, while others have only one pair, and connect this to the definitions of different quadrilateral types.

CC Emerging:
I can identify some basic attributes of two-dimensional shapes, like the number of sides or if it has corners.
Example: When shown a trapezoid, a student can point out its sides and count that it has four. They can also identify that it has some "straight" sides and some "slanted" sides, demonstrating an early understanding of different side properties.

wi.levelDescriptors:
CC Advanced:
I can analyze the properties of two-dimensional shapes to create my own classification systems and explain the reasoning behind my choices.
Example: Instead of using traditional categories, a student might create a hierarchy based on lines of symmetry, grouping shapes with zero lines, one line, two lines, etc. They can justify why they chose this system and how it helps organize shapes.

CC At Target:
I can classify two-dimensional figures into a hierarchy (like a flowchart) based on their properties. I can explain how shapes in the same category share attributes and give examples. Example: A student can create a flowchart where all shapes are first divided into "quadrilaterals" and "not quadrilaterals." Then, within quadrilaterals, they can further categorize them as "parallelograms," "trapezoids," and "other quadrilaterals," explaining the rules for each branch.

CC Approaching:
I can identify and name common two-dimensional shapes. I can sort shapes into groups based on two or more properties and explain my choices.
Example: Given a set of shapes, a student can correctly name a square, rectangle, triangle, circle, trapezoid, pentagon, and hexagon. They can sort the shapes by properties like "number of sides" and "has right angles," explaining their reasoning.

CC Emerging:
I can identify basic two-dimensional shapes like squares, circles, and triangles. I can sort shapes into groups based on a single property, like their color.
Example: When shown a mix of shapes, a student can point out all the triangles. They can also sort shapes by color, putting all the red shapes together.
